# 24BYT408 | Biology for Engineers

**100-mark continuous internal assessment | No end-semester exam | 2 credits**

## Module 1 — Cells, nervous systems and biological engineering

### Why biology matters to mechanical engineers

Living organisms are systems that transport fluids, transfer heat, sense their environment, move using forces and adapt to changing conditions. Mechanical engineers use biological principles in prostheses, medical devices, robotics, fluid pumps, thermal regulation and materials. Biomimetics takes inspiration from biological functions rather than copying an organism blindly. A living system is more complex than a machine: it grows, responds chemically and electrically, repairs itself within limits and maintains internal conditions.

### Cell structure and potential

The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of living organisms. A cell membrane is a selective phospholipid bilayer containing proteins for transport and signaling. Cytoplasm contains organelles; the nucleus houses most DNA in eukaryotic cells; mitochondria help produce ATP through cellular respiration; ribosomes make proteins; endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus process/transport proteins and lipids. Cells maintain different ion concentrations inside and outside. Diffusion moves substances down concentration gradients; facilitated diffusion uses membrane proteins; active transport uses energy to move substances against gradients. Osmosis is net water movement across a selectively permeable membrane driven by chemical potential differences. The resting membrane potential is voltage inside relative to outside, created by unequal ion concentrations and selective permeability. Sodium-potassium pumps move three Na+ out and two K+ in per ATP cycle, helping maintain gradients. Potassium leak channels allow K+ movement; the equilibrium voltage for one ion is given by Nernst equation E=(RT/zF)ln(Cout/Cin), with sign determined by ion charge and concentration ratio.

### Nervous system and machine learning

A neuron has dendrites that receive signals, cell body, axon that conducts impulses and synaptic terminals that communicate with other cells. At threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open causing depolarization; potassium channels then contribute to repolarization. Myelin speeds conduction through saltatory propagation. Chemical synapses release neurotransmitters which bind to receptors; signaling may be excitatory or inhibitory. The central nervous system comprises brain and spinal cord; peripheral nerves connect it to body tissues. Sensory pathways carry information to CNS, motor pathways carry commands to effectors. Reflex arcs provide rapid responses.

*Neuron schematic: signals are received at dendrites, integrated in the cell and transmitted along an axon. (See PDF for the labelled illustration.)*

Artificial neural networks are simplified mathematical systems inspired by connected neurons. An artificial neuron computes weighted sum z=Σwixi+b then activation f(z). Training adjusts weights to reduce a loss on examples; test data evaluate generalization. Supervised learning uses labeled data, unsupervised finds patterns, reinforcement learning uses reward signals. ANN evolution includes perceptrons, multilayer networks and deep learning; these are not literal replicas of a brain. Mechanical applications include vibration-based fault detection, image inspection and predictive maintenance.

### Worked application and assignment

At T=310 K, for K+ concentration outside 5 mmol/L and inside 140 mmol/L, E≈(8.314×310/96,485)ln(5/140)=−0.089 V=−89 mV; actual membrane potential also depends on other ions/permeabilities. A simple artificial neuron with inputs 2 and 1, weights 0.5 and −0.2, bias 0.1 has z=0.9; ReLU output=max(0,z)=0.9. Assignment: draw cell and neuron, explain ion channels and action potential, compare biological and artificial neuron, propose a fault-detection system and list its training/validation data.

## Module 2 — Circulation and respiration

### Heart as a pump

The circulatory system includes heart, blood and vessels. Blood transports oxygen, nutrients, hormones, wastes and heat; red cells carry oxygen, white cells support immune defense, platelets aid clotting and plasma carries dissolved substances. The heart has right/left atria and ventricles; valves promote one-way flow. Body → venae cavae → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve/artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve/aorta → body. The right side supplies lungs; left supplies systemic circulation. Contraction (systole) ejects blood, relaxation (diastole) fills chambers. Stroke volume is blood ejected per beat; cardiac output=heart rate×stroke volume. The sinoatrial node normally initiates electrical activity, atrioventricular node delays conduction, His-Purkinje system distributes impulses. ECG P wave represents atrial depolarization, QRS ventricular depolarization and T ventricular repolarization. ECG records electrical activity, not directly pumping volume.

Blood is a suspension with shear-dependent viscosity in many conditions; large-vessel flow may sometimes be approximated as Newtonian. For steady laminar Newtonian flow through a rigid cylindrical tube, Poiseuille Q=πr⁴Δp/(8μL). Real blood flow is pulsatile, vessels compliant and branching. Narrowing increases resistance and can cause altered flow; coronary blockage can reduce oxygen supply. Blood distributes heat from metabolically active tissues to skin, acting as a biological heat transport fluid; vasodilation increases skin flow, vasoconstriction reduces it.

*Blood flow direction: body to right heart, lungs, left heart and back to body. Not an anatomical cross-section. (See PDF for the labelled illustration.)*

### Lungs and biomedical devices

Respiratory system includes airways, lungs, alveoli, diaphragm and respiratory muscles. During quiet inspiration diaphragm contracts, chest volume increases and pressure falls, drawing air in; passive expiration follows elastic recoil. Oxygen diffuses from alveolar air into pulmonary blood and carbon dioxide in reverse direction according to partial-pressure gradients. Thin moist membrane, large surface and adequate ventilation/perfusion support exchange. Spirometry measures volumes/flows such as FVC and FEV1; interpretation requires reference values and trained staff. A ventilator provides controlled respiratory support using specified pressure/volume and timing, requiring clinical supervision. A heart-lung machine temporarily pumps and oxygenates blood during some surgeries, with heat exchange, monitoring and anticoagulation under specialist control.

### Worked application and assignment

If stroke volume=70 mL and heart rate=75/min, output=5,250 mL/min=5.25 L/min. For a model vessel radius reduced to 80% of original at constant pressure gradient and viscosity, Qnew/Qold=0.8⁴=0.4096. Real circulation can compensate, so do not use this model to diagnose a patient. Assignment: sketch heart circulation; compare heart with a positive-displacement pump and lungs with a gas exchanger; explain ECG waves, blood heat transfer, spirometer and ventilator purpose.

## Module 3 — Kidney filtration, temperature control and sensing

### Urinary system as a separation system

The urinary system includes kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra. Kidneys regulate fluid, electrolytes, acid-base balance and remove wastes; they also have endocrine functions. Nephrons are functional units: glomerulus filters plasma into Bowman's capsule, tubules reabsorb useful substances/water and secrete selected substances; collecting ducts regulate final water content. Filtration depends on pressure differences and selective barriers; blood cells and most large proteins normally remain in circulation. Tubular transport is selective, unlike a simple screen filter. Urine flows via ureters to bladder and leaves through urethra. Hemodialysis removes small solutes through a semipermeable membrane by diffusion and excess fluid by controlled ultrafiltration. Dialysate flows across the membrane with appropriate composition; a clinical machine monitors pressure, conductivity, temperature and safety. Peritoneal dialysis uses the peritoneal membrane. Dialysis only replaces some kidney functions and is medically supervised.

### Biological heat balance

Human metabolism releases heat; some energy becomes external mechanical work. A simplified energy balance is S=M−W−(R+C+K+E), where S stored heat, M metabolic rate, W external work, R radiation, C convection, K conduction and E evaporation; signs depend on heat-flow direction. At steady body heat storage S≈0. Skin blood flow changes heat delivery to surface, sweating increases evaporative loss, shivering generates heat, and behaviour (clothing, shade) changes heat exchange. The hypothalamus coordinates regulation. Humidity limits evaporation; hot surroundings may cause convection/radiation heat gain. Clinical temperature and heat illness require proper medical assessment.

### Sense organs and sensor design

The eye focuses light through cornea and lens onto retina; rods support low-light vision and cones colour/detail; optic nerve carries signals to brain. A digital camera uses lens, aperture, image sensor and processor; retinal adaptation and neural interpretation are more complex. Hearing converts pressure waves through outer/middle ear to vibrations in cochlea, where hair cells transduce them. Skin receptors sense touch, pressure, vibration and temperature; smell/taste involve chemical receptors; vestibular organs sense acceleration and balance. Engineered sensors need sensitivity, range, selectivity, response time, calibration, noise control, drift resistance and safe integration. Bioinspired sensors may use flexible materials, arrays or feedback; they must be tested rather than assumed equivalent to organs.

### Worked application and assignment

For a simplified thermal balance, M=300 W, W=60 W, radiation/convection/conduction loss combined=100 W. Required evaporation to avoid storage=140 W. With latent heat of evaporation 2.4 MJ/kg, fully evaporated water rate=140/2.4×10⁶ kg/s=0.21 kg/h. This is a model, not a hydration prescription; humidity and actual sweat evaporation vary. Assignment: draw nephron and dialysis membrane, compare kidney to industrial filtration, explain body heat control, compare eye and digital camera in a table.

## Module 4 — Musculoskeletal mechanics, prosthetics and biomaterials

### Mechanical function of bones and muscles

The skeleton supports the body, protects organs and provides attachment points. Bone is a living composite: mineral contributes stiffness and collagen contributes toughness. Cortical bone is dense; trabecular bone has porous internal architecture. Bone response depends on direction, rate, density and remodeling. Muscles generate tension, tendons connect muscle to bone, ligaments connect bones and stabilize joints. Synovial joints allow motion with cartilage and synovial fluid reducing friction. Types include hinge (elbow), ball-and-socket (hip/shoulder), pivot and others. Muscles often act through lever arms shorter than the external load arm, producing high muscle forces. Torque=force×perpendicular moment arm; static equilibrium requires sum of moments zero. During motion use dynamics and consider joint reaction forces, acceleration and muscle co-contraction. Muscles cannot generally push; antagonistic muscles provide opposite actions.

*Simplified forearm lever model with perpendicular forces; actual muscle geometry and joint loading are more complex. (See PDF for the labelled illustration.)*

### Assistive engineering and implants

Biomechanics applies mechanics to living systems. Prostheses replace missing body parts; orthoses support or modify an existing body part; exoskeletons assist movement using passive springs or powered actuators with sensors/control. Design objectives include load capacity, comfort, stability, range of motion, low mass, energy efficiency and user safety. Joint alignment and pressure distribution matter; a device must be individualized and clinically evaluated. A biomaterial interacts with biological systems for a medical purpose. Key properties: biocompatibility (appropriate host response for use), mechanical strength, fatigue resistance, modulus, corrosion/wear resistance, surface properties and sterilizability. Titanium alloys offer good corrosion resistance and strength; stainless steels and cobalt-chromium are used for selected implants; polymers such as UHMWPE provide bearing surfaces; ceramics can be hard/wear resistant but brittle; biodegradable materials are selected for controlled degradation. Stress shielding may occur if an implant is much stiffer than bone, reducing normal bone loading. Material selection depends on application, not a universal best material.

### Worked application and assignment

A simplified forearm holds a 30 N load 0.30 m from elbow. Muscle perpendicular moment arm=0.04 m. Neglect arm weight and other muscles; moment balance gives muscle force=30×0.30/0.04=225 N. Joint reaction must also balance forces, showing why internal loads exceed external load. For an implant cross-section 50 mm² under axial force 1,000 N, nominal stress=20 MPa; real design also needs fatigue, stress concentration and biological evaluation. Assignment: compare prosthesis/orthosis/exoskeleton; sketch lever model; select candidate materials for a hip implant and justify properties, risks and testing. Do not treat this as medical device design approval.

## Module 5 — Biomimicry, genetics and evolutionary optimization

### Nature-inspired engineering

Biomimicry abstracts principles from organisms to solve engineering problems. Gecko adhesion uses many fine contact structures and intermolecular forces, inspiring reversible dry adhesives. Spider silk combines strength and toughness through molecular structure and spinning; artificial fibres attempt to reproduce those properties. Bone-inspired lattice materials place material along load paths and reduce mass; leaf-vein networks distribute fluid with branching paths; bird wings inspire airfoil shapes, flexible control and aerodynamic designs. Engineers should define the biological function, identify mechanism, translate it into measurable variables, prototype, test and compare with conventional design. Similar appearance alone is not evidence of functional biomimicry. Evolution produces adaptation to environments through variation, inheritance and selection, not guaranteed global optimum.

### Genetics and genetic algorithms

DNA carries genetic information; a gene is a sequence contributing to a functional product or regulated function; alleles are variants. Genotype is genetic makeup, phenotype observable traits influenced by genes and environment. In a simple Mendelian single-gene model a dominant allele can express the trait in a heterozygote, while a recessive trait requires two recessive alleles; many real traits involve multiple genes, incomplete dominance or other patterns. If two heterozygous Aa parents are crossed, expected genotypes are 1 AA:2 Aa:1 aa, and phenotypes 3:1 under complete dominance and simple assumptions. Natural selection changes frequency of inherited traits linked to reproductive success in an environment.

A genetic algorithm is a computational search: encode design variables as individuals, generate population, evaluate fitness, select parents, recombine through crossover, mutate some variables, preserve useful solutions and repeat until stopping criterion. Constraints may be enforced by repair or penalties. It can search complex nonconvex spaces but may converge prematurely and has no general guarantee of global optimum. Example: optimize a beam cross-section to minimize mass while keeping bending stress/deflection within limits. Fitness could be negative mass minus penalty for violations. Compare multiple random seeds and a baseline analytical solution.

### Worked application and assignment

For an idealized rectangular beam with fixed width b, length L and moment M, mass=ρb hL, stress=6M/(bh²). An optimizer varies height h and rejects designs exceeding σallow. Analytical minimum height from strength alone is √(6M/(bσallow)); also check deflection and available dimensions. A genetic algorithm should recover a feasible near-minimum, not just a low mass violating stress. Assignment: select gecko adhesive, spider silk, bone lattice, leaf network or bird wing; describe biological mechanism, candidate engineered design, test metric and limitations. Draw genetic algorithm flow, solve Aa×Aa cross and explain natural vs computational selection.

**60-mark ESE | 40-mark CIA | 3 credits**

## Module 1 — Bookkeeping and accounting

### Meaning and accounting principles

Bookkeeping records financial transactions; accounting classifies, summarizes, interprets and reports those transactions for decision-making. A mechanical engineer may use accounting to monitor machine cost, inventory, wages, repairs and project profitability. Financial accounting reports to external and internal users; cost accounting measures costs of products or activities; management accounting supports decisions, budgets and performance analysis. Accounting standards promote comparability and reliable presentation (Indian Accounting Standards or applicable AS depend on the entity and legal framework). Core concepts: business entity separates owner and business; going concern assumes continued operation unless evidence indicates otherwise; accrual records income/expense when earned/incurred, not simply on cash receipt/payment; matching associates expenses with related revenue; consistency uses comparable methods; prudence exercises caution without intentional bias; materiality focuses on significant information; disclosure provides necessary context.

### Double-entry system and recording cycle

Assets = liabilities + equity. Every transaction has at least two entries with total debits equal to total credits. Assets and expenses increase on debit; liabilities, equity and revenue increase on credit. Decreases go to the opposite side. Traditional rules: personal accounts debit receiver/credit giver; real accounts debit what comes in/credit what goes out; nominal accounts debit expenses/losses/credit incomes/gains. Use modern account classification when in doubt. Source documents (invoice, receipt, bank record) support journal entries. The journal records transactions chronologically. Ledger groups by account; balance each account and transfer balances to trial balance. A trial balance checks debit/credit arithmetic but cannot detect every error, e.g. complete omission or equal wrong-account entries.

### Worked example — Journal to trial balance

A workshop starts with cash ₹50,000; buys equipment for ₹20,000 cash; buys materials on credit ₹8,000; performs a cash service ₹12,000; pays wages ₹3,000; pays supplier ₹2,000. Journal: Dr Cash 50,000 / Cr Capital 50,000; Dr Equipment 20,000 / Cr Cash 20,000; Dr Inventory 8,000 / Cr Payables 8,000; Dr Cash 12,000 / Cr Service revenue 12,000; Dr Wages 3,000 / Cr Cash 3,000; Dr Payables 2,000 / Cr Cash 2,000. Ledger balances: Cash 37,000 Dr; Equipment 20,000 Dr; Inventory 8,000 Dr; Wages 3,000 Dr; Payables 6,000 Cr; Capital 50,000 Cr; Revenue 12,000 Cr. Trial balance totals ₹68,000 on each side. Assume the inventory is unused. Keep supporting documents and never falsify transactions.

### Exam practice

Distinguish bookkeeping and accounting; explain five concepts with examples; prepare journal, ledger and trial balance from the example. Practice: purchase a machine for ₹10,000 on credit. Answer Dr Equipment ₹10,000, Cr Payables ₹10,000; no immediate cash movement.

## Module 2 — Financial statements and accounting software

### Profit and loss account and balance sheet

The income statement measures performance during a period: revenue minus expenses = profit or loss. For trading, cost of goods sold = opening inventory + net purchases + direct expenses − closing inventory; gross profit = net sales − COGS; net profit = gross profit + other income − operating and other expenses. Accrual adjustments include outstanding expenses (expense and liability), prepaid expenses (asset), depreciation (noncash expense and reduction of carrying value), accrued income and unearned revenue. Balance sheet shows financial position at a date: assets (current and noncurrent), liabilities and equity. It is not a statement of market value. Depreciation allocates depreciable amount over useful life; straight-line annual amount=(cost−residual value)/life.

### Cash flow statement

Cash flow classifies actual cash movements: operating (main business activities), investing (purchase/sale of long-term assets or investments) and financing (capital contributions, borrowings and repayments, distributions as applicable). Profit differs from cash because of credit transactions, depreciation and working capital changes. In indirect operating cash flow, start with relevant profit and adjust noncash items, items belonging to investing/financing, and changes in working capital. Increase in inventory or receivables generally reduces operating cash; increase in trade payables generally increases it. Cash opening + net flow = closing cash. Classification for interest/dividends depends on applicable standards and entity.

### Worked example — Complete statements

Use Module 1 transactions, with unused inventory, and record ₹2,000 depreciation. Revenue ₹12,000; wages ₹3,000; depreciation ₹2,000; profit ₹7,000. Balance sheet: cash 37,000 + inventory 8,000 + equipment net 18,000 = assets ₹63,000. Payables ₹6,000 + capital 50,000 + profit 7,000 = ₹63,000. Cash flow: operating receipts 12,000 less wages 3,000 and supplier payment 2,000 = ₹7,000; investing −20,000; financing +50,000; net cash +37,000. Indirect check: profit 7,000 + depreciation 2,000 − inventory increase 8,000 + payable increase 6,000 = 7,000.

### Accounting software workflow

In a training company in Tally, Zoho Books or another tool, set reporting period and chart of accounts, create supplier/customer/items, enter opening balances and vouchers (sales, purchases, receipts, payments, journals), reconcile bank, record adjustments, and export trial balance, P&L and balance sheet. Example: record the six transactions, compare reports with manual results. Use fictional training data, not real customer details. Taxes are excluded in the example; apply actual tax rules only with correct settings.

### Exam practice

Explain all three cash flow categories with examples. Prepare statements from trial balance and adjustments. Explain why depreciation reduces profit but is not a cash payment in that period.

## Module 3 — Financial management and investment concepts

### Objectives and decisions

Financial management plans, obtains and uses funds efficiently. Main decisions concern investment in assets, sources of finance and distribution/retention of earnings. Profit maximization emphasizes earnings; wealth maximization considers risk, timing and sustainable value. Financial planning sets funding requirements and cash projections; control compares results with plans and takes corrective action. A portfolio combines assets; diversification reduces asset-specific risk but not all market risk. Expected portfolio return = ΣwiRi, with weights summing to one; risk also depends on covariance, not only individual risks. Financing decision balances cost, control and risk; dividend decision balances distributions against retained funds for growth.

### Ratios and asset categories

Liquidity: current ratio=current assets/current liabilities; quick ratio=(cash+short-term liquid investments+receivables)/current liabilities. Leverage: debt-to-equity=defined debt/equity; interest coverage=EBIT/interest expense. Efficiency: inventory turnover=COGS/average inventory; receivables turnover=credit sales/average receivables; asset turnover=sales/average assets. Profitability: gross margin=gross profit/sales, net margin=net profit/sales, ROA=profit/average assets and ROE=profit attributable to owners/average equity. Market ratios: EPS=earnings attributable to ordinary shareholders/weighted average shares; P/E=share price/EPS (interpret cautiously for negative earnings). Ratios need comparable periods, industry and definitions.

Long-term investment examples in syllabus: gold (no operating cash flow), equity (ownership and risk), bonds (debt claims), real estate (illiquidity/maintenance), investments in other companies; PPF and NPS are Indian long-term savings/retirement schemes with eligibility and withdrawal rules. Trademarks and patents are intellectual property with legal rights, not guaranteed investment returns. Short-term products include money-market accounts, high-yield savings, government bonds of suitable maturity and treasury bills (short-term government debt). Compare liquidity, maturity, risk, expected return, costs and legal/ethical constraints. These are academic definitions, not personal investment recommendations. Case study: Abakkus fund and Sunil Singhania — investigate official fund documents, investment process, concentration, disclosed risk and benchmarks rather than assuming past returns predict future outcomes.

### Worked example

Current assets ₹120,000, inventory ₹40,000, current liabilities ₹60,000, equity ₹150,000, debt ₹75,000, sales ₹200,000, net profit ₹20,000. Current ratio=2; quick ratio=(120,000−40,000)/60,000=1.33 if other assets are liquid; debt/equity=0.5; net margin=10%. A portfolio with 60% expected return 8% and 40% expected return 4% has expected return 6.4%, not a guaranteed return.

### Exam practice

Compare profit and wealth maximization; classify ratios and explain interpretation; discuss long/short-term assets, diversification, financial planning and dividend decisions. For a ratio answer show formula, substitution, result and interpretation.

## Module 4 — Banking systems

### Banking functions and structure

Banks accept deposits, provide payment services, lend and facilitate transfers. The Reserve Bank of India is the central bank, distinct from commercial banks. Scheduled commercial banks, cooperative banks, regional rural banks, small finance banks and payments banks serve different roles and operate under applicable regulations. Rural financing supports agriculture, microenterprise and households; accessible branches, digital payments and responsible credit can improve inclusion. Banker-customer relationships differ by service: deposit generally creates debtor-creditor relationship (bank owes customer); loans reverse the roles; collection/agency and custody services create other obligations. Customer satisfaction depends on transparent charges, security, timely services, accessibility, grievance redressal and confidentiality. KYC and anti-money-laundering compliance protect the system; do not share OTPs or PINs. Academic study of interest-based products is separate from personal ethical choices.

### Balance sheet and transfers

For a bank, deposits are liabilities because they are owed to depositors; loans are assets because borrowers owe the bank. Cash/reserves and investments are also assets. Deposit mobilization means collecting savings/current/term deposits; lending may be secured or unsecured, short- or long-term. Credit appraisal assesses repayment ability, collateral where applicable and risk; bad loans reduce asset quality. Cheque endorsement involves signing to transfer or authorize payment subject to law and cheque terms. Crossing generally directs payment through a bank rather than over the counter; account-payee crossing restricts collection to named payee. Electronic transfers include NEFT (batch-based settlement), RTGS (real-time gross settlement), IMPS and UPI (instant-payment mechanisms). Refer to official RBI/NPCI rules for limits, timing and charges rather than memorizing outdated figures.

### Case study — Washington Mutual, 2008

Washington Mutual failed in September 2008 amid mortgage-related losses, funding pressure and a loss of depositor confidence; US regulators closed the bank and the FDIC arranged a sale of banking operations to JPMorgan Chase. Lessons: underwriting, liquidity buffers, concentration risk, governance, supervision and confidence all matter. A bank can face liquidity pressure even when it reports assets, because assets may be hard to sell quickly. Do not confuse liquidity with solvency. Read the FDIC official release for exact case details.

### Worked example and exam practice

A simplified bank has deposits 900, equity 100, cash/reserves 150, loans 700 and investments 150 (₹ lakh). Assets=1,000; liabilities+equity=1,000. A withdrawal of 100 reduces cash/reserves to 50 and deposits to 800; the balance sheet still balances but liquidity falls. Explain types and functions of banks, banker-customer relationship, deposit mobilization, cheque crossing and digital transfer distinctions. Design a customer satisfaction survey with consent, anonymous responses and clear questions.

## Module 5 — Budgeting and budget analysis

### Budget basics

A budget is a quantified plan for a future period. It coordinates resources, assigns responsibility and controls spending. Expenditure is spending; a deficit arises when relevant spending exceeds relevant receipts. In public finance, fiscal deficit = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts), indicating borrowing requirement under the standard Indian definition. Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts. A balanced budget has receipts equal to expenditure on the defined basis, surplus has more receipts, deficit has less. Union and State budgets relate to their respective governments. Distinguish government borrowing from a firm's operating loss.

### Types and approaches

Master budget combines functional budgets; operating budget includes sales, production and expenses; financial budget includes cash, capital and projected position; cash budget schedules cash receipts/payments; static budget uses one activity level; flexible budget adjusts variable costs to actual activity; capital expenditure budget covers long-term assets; program budgets allocate by programs/outcomes; zero-based budgeting requires justification from a zero base. Activity-based budgeting estimates activity demands and resource costs; add-on/incremental adds adjustments to previous budget; bracket prepares multiple scenarios; rolling budget extends horizon as time passes; rolling forecast updates expectations rather than fixed targets; strategic budget aligns with strategy; stretch sets ambitious but realistic targets; supplemental adjusts approved resources; target budget works toward an assigned spending or performance goal. Analyze budget variances by frequency, cause, revised forecast and corrective action. A favorable cost variance is actual below budget, but poor quality may make it unfavorable overall.

### Worked example — Cash and flexible budget

Opening cash ₹20,000, expected collections ₹50,000, wages ₹18,000, materials ₹22,000, equipment purchase ₹15,000. Closing cash=20,000+50,000−18,000−22,000−15,000=₹15,000. If required buffer ₹20,000, shortfall ₹5,000. For flexible budget fixed cost ₹30,000 and variable cost ₹20/unit at planned 1,000 units, static budget=₹50,000. Actual output 1,200 gives flexible budget ₹54,000. If actual cost ₹56,000, spending variance ₹2,000 unfavorable; difference ₹6,000 from static budget includes ₹4,000 activity effect. Government example: expenditure 1,000, revenue receipts 700, non-debt capital receipts 50, revenue expenditure 800 (same units); fiscal deficit=250, revenue deficit=100.

### Exam practice

Compare static and flexible budget, explain master/cash/capital budgets and zero-based approach; calculate fiscal and revenue deficits; analyse a budget variance with corrective action. For the Union Budget assignment use the official budget for the assigned year and cite documents, do not invent current totals.

# 24MCT406 | Environmental Sciences

**60-mark ESE | 40-mark CIA | Mandatory course (1 credit as listed)**

## Module 1 — Environment, biodiversity and sustainability

### Ecosystems and human dependence

Environmental science studies interactions among living organisms, physical surroundings and human activities. It combines ecology, chemistry, engineering, economics, public health and ethics. An ecosystem contains biotic components (plants, animals, microbes) and abiotic components (light, air, water, soil, temperature). Producers convert solar energy into organic matter, consumers obtain energy through feeding, decomposers break down dead matter and recycle nutrients. Energy flows through trophic levels and dissipates as heat; elements cycle through water, carbon and nitrogen cycles. A food web is more realistic than a single food chain. Ecosystem services include provisioning (food, water), regulating (flood control, pollination, climate), cultural and supporting functions. Mangroves reduce wave energy, trap sediments, store carbon and provide nursery habitats; their protective effectiveness depends on width, density and local conditions.

Biodiversity includes genetic variation within species, species diversity and ecosystem diversity. It supports resilience, crop improvement, medicines and ecosystem function. Habitat loss/fragmentation, invasive species, overexploitation, pollution and climate change threaten biodiversity. In-situ conservation protects habitats (protected areas, community reserves); ex-situ methods protect organisms outside their habitats (seed banks, botanical gardens). Conservation should also respect local livelihoods. Health and environment interact through clean water, sanitation, air quality, heat, food safety and occupational exposure. Environmental ethics addresses responsibility to future generations, other species and affected communities; polluter-pays and precautionary approaches are useful principles.

### Sustainable development

Sustainable development meets present needs without undermining future generations' ability to meet theirs. Three connected dimensions are social equity, economic viability and environmental protection. For mechanical engineers, examples include energy-efficient equipment, repairable products, safe working conditions, material recovery and lifecycle assessment. The UN's 17 SDGs include clean water (6), clean energy (7), decent work (8), industry and infrastructure (9), sustainable cities (11), responsible consumption (12), climate action (13), life below water (14) and life on land (15), along with other social and governance goals. Trade-offs must be measured: an efficient device may still be harmful if produced using hazardous methods or used excessively.

### Worked application and exam answer

A campus wetland is threatened by dumping and construction. Explain consequences: loss of habitat reduces biodiversity; blocked drainage increases flood risk; nutrient input causes algal growth and oxygen depletion. Actions: protect buffer zone, stop dumping, treat wastewater, monitor species/water quality and involve the community. Exam question: explain the structure and functions of an ecosystem with a food-chain sketch (sun → grass → grasshopper → frog; decomposers return nutrients). Define biodiversity at three levels, distinguish in-situ/ex-situ and explain the three sustainability dimensions with an engineering example.

## Module 2 — Air and noise pollution

### Air pollutants and impacts

Primary pollutants are emitted directly (CO, SO2, NOx, particulate matter, VOCs); secondary pollutants form in the atmosphere (ground-level ozone, secondary particles). Combustion in engines and industries emits NOx and particles; sulfur in fuel produces SO2; incomplete combustion produces CO, which reduces blood oxygen transport. PM2.5 penetrates deep into lungs and is associated with cardiovascular and respiratory harm. NOx and VOCs in sunlight form photochemical smog, including ozone; ground-level ozone harms lungs and vegetation. Stratospheric ozone is beneficial because it absorbs UV radiation. CFCs and related ozone-depleting substances release reactive halogens in the stratosphere; the Montreal Protocol controls these substances. Global warming is a different problem caused by greenhouse gases trapping outgoing infrared radiation. Some chemicals contribute to both problems.

Air pollution control includes cleaner fuels and electrification where beneficial, process modification, combustion optimization, cyclones/bag filters/electrostatic precipitators for particles, scrubbers for certain gases, and catalytic controls. Indoor air quality depends on ventilation, moisture/mould, cooking emissions, dust, VOCs and occupancy; control sources and ventilate appropriately. India's Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act provides a legal framework; NAAQS specify pollutant-specific ambient concentrations and averaging times. AQI converts concentrations to health-oriented sub-indices; the overall index is generally the worst available valid sub-index under the CPCB method. For exact current values and averaging rules use CPCB, not generic international limits.

### Noise and quantification

Noise is unwanted sound. Sources include traffic, compressors, machines and construction. Prolonged exposure may damage hearing and affect sleep, stress and communication. Sound pressure level Lp=20 log10(p/p0), with p0=20 µPa in air. For independent sound sources combine energies: Ltotal=10 log10 Σ10^(Li/10). Leq is the energy-equivalent constant level over time; for discrete durations Leq=10 log10[Σti10^(Li/10)/Σti]. LAeq uses A-frequency weighting to approximate hearing response. Control at source (quiet equipment, balancing), path (enclosures, barriers, isolation) and receiver (hearing protection). Indian Noise Pollution Rules distinguish zones and day/night; consult current CPCB/MoEFCC rules for legal limits.

### Worked example

Two independent sources each at 80 dB produce 10 log10(2×10⁸)=83.01 dB, not 160 dB. For 30 min at 70 dB and 30 min at 90 dB, Leq=10 log10[(10⁷+10⁹)/2]=87.03 dB. The loud period dominates energy. Exam practice: explain smog formation, indoor air quality, ozone depletion vs climate change, and noise control with industrial examples.

## Module 3 — Water quality, treatment and conservation

### Freshwater and pollution

Freshwater comes from rivers, lakes, reservoirs and groundwater, distributed unevenly and seasonally. Conservation includes leakage reduction, rainwater harvesting, efficient irrigation, reuse of treated water and watershed protection. Competing agricultural, industrial and domestic uses can create conflicts; equitable allocation, demand management and monitoring help. Water pollutants include suspended solids, pathogens, nutrients, metals, oils and organic chemicals. Eutrophication occurs when excess nutrients promote algal growth, whose decomposition consumes dissolved oxygen. DO indicates oxygen available in water; BOD measures oxygen used biologically under specified conditions (e.g., BOD5); COD measures chemically oxidizable matter; turbidity measures cloudiness; pH indicates acidity/alkalinity; TDS describes dissolved solids. Drinking-water standards such as IS 10500 specify parameter limits and test requirements; check the current BIS text. A water quality index combines selected parameters using defined weights/ratings; WQI=Σwiqi/Σwi is one weighted approach, not a universal index.

### Treatment of drinking water and wastewater

Conventional water treatment: intake/screening → coagulation and flocculation (destabilize and aggregate particles) → sedimentation (settle flocs) → filtration (remove remaining particles) → disinfection (control pathogens) → safe storage/distribution. Treatment depends on raw water; dissolved salts or specific chemicals may need additional processes. Wastewater comes from homes, commerce and industry. Primary treatment screens, removes grit and settles solids. Secondary treatment uses microorganisms (activated sludge, trickling filters) to remove biodegradable organics; a secondary clarifier separates biomass. Tertiary/advanced treatment removes nutrients, fine solids or specific pollutants and may disinfect for reuse/discharge. Sludge needs safe treatment and disposal. Decentralized systems include septic/anaerobic treatment with suitable soil or further treatment, packaged plants and constructed wetlands. Natural methods use ponds and vegetation/microbes, needing area, suitable climate and maintenance. Discharge must satisfy applicable standards and permits.

*Conventional drinking-water treatment sequence. Actual disinfection and process selection depend on source water. (See PDF for the labelled illustration.)*

### Oxygen sag and worked example

When organic waste enters a river, microbes consume DO (deoxygenation) while air-water exchange replenishes it (reaeration). DO initially falls and recovers downstream if conditions allow; oxygen deficit D=DOsat−DO. Streeter–Phelps model dD/dt=k1L−k2D with remaining ultimate BOD L=L0 exp(−k1t). The critical point occurs when deoxygenation equals reaeration. Assume complete immediate mixing and simple first-order rates. If DOsat=9 mg/L and measured DO=5 mg/L, deficit=4 mg/L. If wastewater flow is 100 m³/day with BOD=200 mg/L, load=100,000 L/day×200 mg/L=20 kg/day. A plant removing 90% leaves 2 kg/day at same flow; compliance still requires checking concentration and other parameters.

### Exam practice

Draw and explain drinking-water and sewage treatment flow sheets; discuss BOD vs COD and DO; explain oxygen sag curve; compare centralized and decentralized treatment; describe water conservation and conflicts. Never assume clear-looking water is safe to drink.

## Module 4 — Solid, hazardous and biomedical waste

### Municipal waste and circular economy

Consumerism and a throw-away culture increase resource extraction and disposal. Municipal solid waste may include organics, paper, plastic, glass, metals, inert material and domestic hazardous items. Characterization includes quantity, moisture, density, composition and calorific value. CPHEEO guidance addresses collection, segregation, transport, processing and sanitary disposal; use official manuals and local rules. Waste hierarchy prioritizes prevention, reduction, reuse, repair and recycling, then recovery and safe disposal. A circular economy designs products for durability, disassembly and material circulation, unlike a linear take-make-dispose model. Zero-waste lifestyle emphasizes avoiding unnecessary materials, reuse and source separation; it does not mean every residual can be recycled.

Composting aerobically converts segregated organics into stabilized material; anaerobic digestion yields biogas and digestate needing quality management. Recycling recovers sorted paper/metals/plastic/glass, depending on contamination and markets. Sanitary landfill uses engineered liners, leachate management, gas collection, cover and monitoring; open dumping lacks these safeguards. Incineration thermally treats suitable waste with air pollution controls and ash management. Waste-to-energy includes anaerobic digestion, combustion with energy recovery and other thermal methods; high moisture and poor segregation can undermine performance. Hazardous waste may be toxic, corrosive, reactive or ignitable; identify, label, segregate, store safely and use authorized transport/treatment. E-waste contains valuable metals and hazardous constituents; authorized recycling and producer responsibility reduce unsafe dismantling. Biomedical waste must be segregated at source, handled under applicable colour-category rules and treated by authorized facilities; sharps need puncture-resistant containment. Do not mix medical/hazardous waste with ordinary waste. Check current Indian Solid Waste, Hazardous Waste, E-Waste and Biomedical Waste rules via MoEFCC/CPCB.

### Worked application

A campus generates 100 kg/day: 55 kg organic, 25 recyclable dry, 15 residual and 5 special waste. If 80% organic is composted and 60% recyclables recovered, diversion=44+15=59 kg/day. Remaining 41 kg/day includes 5 kg special waste requiring authorized handling, not landfill by default. Identify why the recovery percentages and destination matter. Exam: explain waste hierarchy, sanitary landfill with sketch (liner, leachate, waste, cover, gas collection), composting vs digestion, e-waste and biomedical handling. Compare environmental impacts of landfill and incineration.

## Module 5 — Climate action and renewable energy

### Climate change and international response

Evidence includes increasing global temperature, ocean warming, changing precipitation patterns, sea-level rise and ice loss. Human greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels, land use and industrial processes are the main driver of recent global warming. Effects include heat stress, changes in flood/drought risk, impacts on agriculture, ecosystems and infrastructure. Carbon footprint expresses relevant emissions in CO2-equivalent using stated system boundary and period. Global warming potential compares integrated radiative effects over a chosen time horizon; values depend on assessment and horizon. IPCC assesses published science; it is not a regulator. UNFCCC is the international climate framework; Kyoto established binding targets for participating developed countries under its arrangements; Paris Agreement uses nationally determined contributions and aims to hold warming well below 2°C and pursue 1.5°C. Mitigation reduces emissions or enhances sinks; adaptation reduces vulnerability to impacts. Carbon capture, utilization and storage captures CO2, transports it and uses or stores it; net benefit depends on energy demand, permanence and lifecycle assessment. Adaptation includes flood-resilient infrastructure, heat plans, efficient cooling and water management.

### Energy technologies

Solar PV converts light to electricity; solar thermal collects heat. Output depends on irradiance, area, efficiency and losses; storage/grid connection manage variability. Wind turbine power available in air=½ρAv³; actual shaft power includes power coefficient Cp (ideal Betz limit 16/27), plus generator losses. Biomass energy can come from residues via combustion or biogas; sustainability depends on feedstock, land use, emissions and supply. Other sources include geothermal, ocean energy, small hydro and hydrogen as an energy carrier (not automatically renewable; depends on production). Renewable energy still has lifecycle material, land and maintenance impacts. Engineering efficiency and demand reduction complement clean generation.

### Worked examples

A solar array area 10 m² receives 800 W/m²; efficiency 20%, instantaneous DC output=800×10×0.20=1,600 W. At an assumed 5 equivalent peak sun hours per day and 80% system performance, a 2 kWp rated system yields 8 kWh/day. For a wind rotor area 50 m², air density 1.2 kg/m³, speed 8 m/s and Cp=0.35, shaft power=0.5×1.2×50×512×0.35=5,376 W. For 100 kWh electricity and a hypothetical emission factor 0.7 kg CO2e/kWh, emissions=70 kg CO2e; use verified regional factor for real assessment.

### Exam practice

Distinguish mitigation and adaptation with examples; explain role of IPCC and three climate agreements; discuss carbon footprint and CCUS; compare solar, wind and biomass with advantages and limitations. Explain how mechanical engineers reduce lifecycle emissions through efficient design, maintenance and material selection.

**40-mark ESE | 60-mark CIA | 5 credits | includes laboratory and project**

## Module 1 — Heat transfer and conduction

### Understanding heat flow

Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Conduction transfers energy through a material without bulk motion; convection combines conduction at a surface with fluid motion; radiation is energy carried by electromagnetic waves. An air conditioner transfers heat from a cool room to the warmer outside by consuming work; a direct evaporative air cooler uses evaporation to cool air and raises humidity. A real machine often involves all three modes. Heat rate Q is measured in W; heat flux q″ in W/m².

### Fourier law and general equation

Fourier's law in one direction is q″ = −k dT/dx, where k is thermal conductivity in W/(m·K). The minus sign indicates heat travels toward lower temperature. Apply energy conservation to a small control volume: net conduction in + internal generation = energy stored. In Cartesian coordinates, ∂(k∂T/∂x)/∂x + ∂(k∂T/∂y)/∂y + ∂(k∂T/∂z)/∂z + q̇g = ρcp ∂T/∂t. For constant k, ∇²T + q̇g/k = (1/α)∂T/∂t, with diffusivity α = k/(ρcp). At steady state without generation and in 1D, d²T/dx²=0, so a plane wall has linear temperature profile. With uniform generation, the profile is parabolic. For steady radial conduction through a cylinder without generation, (1/r)d/dr(r dT/dr)=0, so T=C1 ln r+C2.

### Thermal resistance networks

For a plane wall, Rcond=L/(kA); for cylindrical insulation, Rcond=ln(r2/r1)/(2πkL); film resistance Rconv=1/(hA). Resistances in series add; parallel conductances add. Q=(Th−Tc)/Rtotal. Temperature drops across resistances are Q R. Contact resistance may matter. Insulating a cylinder increases conduction resistance but also outer convection area. Differentiate total resistance with respect to outer radius: critical radius rcrit=k/h. Below that radius, adding insulation may initially increase heat loss; above it, insulation decreases heat loss. This assumes constant k and h and negligible end effects. For spheres rcrit=2k/h, as an extension.

*Composite wall with two film resistances and two solid layers. Temperature line is qualitative. (See PDF for the labelled illustration.)*

### Worked example 1 — Composite wall

A wall of area 2 m² has 0.10 m brick (k=0.8) and 0.05 m insulation (k=0.04). Inside h=10 and outside h=20 W/m²K. Air temperatures are 50 and 20°C. Rtotal=1/(10×2)+0.10/(0.8×2)+0.05/(0.04×2)+1/(20×2)=0.7625 K/W. Q=30/0.7625=39.34 W. Inner surface temperature=50−39.34×0.05=48.03°C. Heat flux=19.67 W/m².

### Worked example 2 — Critical radius

Insulation k=0.06 W/mK and outside h=10 W/m²K gives rcrit=0.006 m=6 mm. If the bare wire radius is 2 mm, adding insulation until 6 mm increases heat loss under the assumptions. Above 6 mm further insulation reduces heat loss.

### Exam and practical work

Derive the general heat conduction equation using a differential control volume. Derive cylindrical resistance and critical radius. For simulation use prescribed temperature/heat flux/convection boundaries, mesh refinement and energy balance; compare predicted heat rate with an analytical benchmark. In lab, measure steady temperatures, power and dimensions; correct for losses before reporting k.

## Module 2 — Convection and lumped transient analysis

### Fluid flow near a surface

Convection depends on motion and temperature difference. Newton's cooling law Q=hAs(Ts−T∞) defines the convection coefficient h; it is not a universal fluid property. Forced convection uses a fan or pump; natural convection arises from buoyancy caused by density variations. At a solid wall, velocity obeys no slip, forming a velocity boundary layer; temperature changes within a thermal boundary layer. Laminar flow has orderly layers; turbulent flow mixes strongly and often increases heat transfer. External flow passes over a plate/cylinder; internal flow is confined in a duct. Internal flow may be developing or fully developed, thermally and hydrodynamically.

### Dimensionless numbers and correlations

Re=ρVL/μ compares inertia and viscosity; Pr=ν/α compares momentum and thermal diffusivity; Nu=hL/k measures convection relative to conduction; Gr=gβΔTL³/ν² compares buoyancy and viscosity; Ra=GrPr. Choose the characteristic length and fluid properties as specified by the correlation. For a laminar isothermal flat plate, average NuL=0.664 ReL^0.5 Pr^1/3 (common range ReL below about 5×10⁵, Pr≥0.6; check applicable range). For fully developed laminar circular tube flow with constant wall temperature Nu=3.66, or 4.36 for constant wall heat flux. For turbulent smooth tube flow, Dittus–Boelter Nu=0.023 Re^0.8 Prⁿ, n=0.4 for fluid heating and 0.3 for cooling, typical range Re>10,000 and suitable Pr and L/D. For natural convection on a vertical isothermal plate, a common laminar estimate Nu=0.59 Ra^1/4 for about 10⁴–10⁹. Use appropriate validated correlations for other shapes, ranges and turbulent natural convection; never use a pipe correlation on an external plate without justification.

### Lumped heat capacity

If Bi=hLc/ks <0.1 (Lc=volume/surface area), internal temperature gradients are small. Energy balance ρVcp dT/dt=−hAs(T−T∞) leads to (T−T∞)/(Ti−T∞)=exp[−hAs t/(ρVcp)]. Time constant τ=ρVcp/(hAs). Fourier number Fo=αt/Lc² describes transient diffusion. If Bi is large, solve the transient conduction equation or use appropriate charts/numerics.

### Worked examples

Air at a plate: L=0.5 m, velocity=2 m/s, ν=1.5×10⁻⁵ m²/s, Pr=0.71, k=0.026 W/mK. ReL=66,667 (laminar), NuL≈0.664×258.2×0.892=152.9. h=152.9×0.026/0.5=7.95 W/m²K. For A=0.5 m² and ΔT=30 K, Q≈119 W. For a small metal piece with mass 0.2 kg, cp=500 J/kgK, hA=2 W/K, τ=50 s. Cooling from 100°C to 40°C in 20°C air takes t=−50 ln(20/80)=69.3 s, if lumped condition holds.

### Exam and lab

Explain Re, Pr, Nu, Gr, Ra and Bi; compare natural/forced convection. Estimate h from a lab heater input minus losses divided by area and temperature difference. Plot h against air speed; compare with a suitable correlation. In CFD, specify inlet flow, wall temperature, outlet, turbulence model and mesh independence.

## Module 3 — Thermal radiation

### Fundamentals and properties

All bodies above absolute zero emit radiation. Incident radiation is absorbed, reflected or transmitted: αr+ρr+τr=1. Opaque surfaces have τr=0. A blackbody absorbs all incident radiation and has maximum possible thermal emission at its temperature. Emissivity ε is actual emission relative to blackbody emission; a grey surface has wavelength-independent idealized emissivity. Kirchhoff's law relates emissivity and absorptivity at thermal equilibrium for corresponding spectral and directional conditions. Stefan–Boltzmann law Eb=σSB T⁴, σSB=5.670374419×10⁻⁸ W/m²K⁴. Always use Kelvin. Wien's law λmax T≈2898 µm·K describes the blackbody peak wavelength.

### Exchange between surfaces

A view factor Fij is fraction of radiation leaving surface i that directly reaches j. Reciprocity AiFij=AjFji; for a closed enclosure ΣjFij=1. A flat/convex surface has Fii=0; a concave surface can see itself. Irradiation G is incoming radiation; radiosity J is total outgoing radiation (emitted plus reflected). For an opaque diffuse-grey surface J=εEb+(1−ε)G. Net heat rate Qi=Ai(Ji−Gi). For two large parallel diffuse-grey plates, edge effects negligible, Q/A=σSB(T1⁴−T2⁴)/(1/ε1+1/ε2−1). For general two-surface enclosure, Q=(Eb1−Eb2)/[(1−ε1)/(A1ε1)+1/(A1F12)+(1−ε2)/(A2ε2)]. For many surfaces solve radiosity equations using Gi=ΣjFijJj. Radiation shields add surface and space resistances; a low-emissivity shield reduces exchange without necessarily stopping convection or conduction.

*Radiation shield between two large parallel plates adds radiation exchange resistance. (See PDF for the labelled illustration.)*

### Worked examples

Two large plates at 500 K and 300 K, ε1=0.8, ε2=0.6. Numerator σSB(500⁴−300⁴)≈3,084.7 W/m². Denominator=1.25+1.667−1=1.917. Net flux≈1,609 W/m². If both were black, flux would be 3,085 W/m². With one shield of emissivity 0.1 on both faces, series denominator becomes (1/0.8+1/0.1−1)+(1/0.1+1/0.6−1)=20.917. Flux≈147.5 W/m². Assume parallel geometry, vacuum or nonparticipating gap and negligible edge effects.

### Exam and laboratory

Define blackbody, grey body, emissivity, view factor, radiosity and irradiation. Derive the two-plate exchange formula with surface and space resistances. Describe a radiation shield. In lab compare surfaces at measured temperatures and known geometry; correct convection/conduction losses and background radiation. Use Kelvin in every fourth-power calculation. For simulation verify view-factor sums and energy balance.

## Module 4 — Heat exchangers, boiling and condensation

### Heat exchanger arrangements

A heat exchanger transfers energy between fluid streams, usually without mixing. Parallel flow streams move in the same direction, counterflow in opposite directions, crossflow perpendicular; shell-and-tube and plate exchangers provide large area. For negligible losses and no phase change, Q=mh cph(Thi−Tho)=mc cpc(Tco−Tci). The overall coefficient U includes film, wall and fouling resistances. Q=UA F ΔTlm where F is a correction factor for multi-pass/crossflow configurations, and ΔTlm=(ΔT1−ΔT2)/ln(ΔT1/ΔT2). For equal end differences use that common difference. Match temperatures to the correct end. Counterflow can achieve a cold outlet warmer than the hot outlet without violating local heat-flow direction.

*Counterflow heat exchanger with temperatures from the worked example. Streams do not mix. (See PDF for the labelled illustration.)*

### Effectiveness–NTU method

C=ṁcp is heat capacity rate, Cmin is smaller rate, Cr=Cmin/Cmax. Qmax=Cmin(Thi−Tci). Effectiveness ε=Q/Qmax and NTU=UA/Cmin. Parallel-flow ε=[1−exp(−NTU(1+Cr))]/(1+Cr). Counterflow ε=[1−exp(−NTU(1−Cr))]/[1−Cr exp(−NTU(1−Cr))] for Cr≠1; for Cr=1, ε=NTU/(1+NTU). Choose this method if outlet temperatures are unknown. Select exchanger by duty, pressure drop, fouling, material compatibility, operating pressure, cleaning and cost.

### Boiling and condensation

In pool boiling the liquid is initially stationary; flow boiling occurs in moving fluid. The pool-boiling curve shows natural convection, nucleate boiling, critical heat flux, transition boiling and film boiling. Nucleate bubbles enhance transfer; beyond critical heat flux a vapour blanket may form, sharply increasing surface temperature. Film condensation forms a liquid layer that resists heat flow; dropwise condensation often gives higher h but is difficult to maintain. For a laminar condensate film on a vertical plate, average Nusselt theory gives h≈0.943[ρl(ρl−ρv)g hfg kl³/(μl L ΔT)]^1/4 under its assumptions. During phase change Q=ṁhfg if only latent heat is exchanged. In design, avoid dryout and check condensate drainage.

*Qualitative pool-boiling curve. CHF is critical heat flux; the transition region is unstable in many heat-flux-controlled systems. (See PDF for the labelled illustration.)*

### Worked example

Counterflow: hot water 0.5 kg/s from 80 to 60°C, cold water enters at 20°C at 1 kg/s, cp=4,180 J/kgK. Q=41,800 W; cold outlet=20+41,800/4,180=30°C. End differences 80−30=50 K, 60−20=40 K; LMTD=10/ln(50/40)=44.81 K. If U=500 W/m²K, A=41,800/(500×44.81)=1.866 m². Cmin=2,090 W/K, Qmax=125,400 W, ε=1/3. A 5 kW condenser removing latent heat 2,250 kJ/kg condenses 0.00222 kg/s.

### Exam and lab

Derive LMTD using differential heat balance; state assumptions. Compare LMTD and NTU methods. Sketch boiling curve and label critical heat flux. In lab measure both flow rates and all four temperatures, calculate hot/cold heat rates, discrepancy, LMTD, U and effectiveness; avoid claiming exact energy balance when there are losses.

## Module 5 — Mass transfer

### Diffusion and convection

Mass transfer occurs due to concentration or chemical-potential differences, e.g. evaporation from a cooling tower, diffusion of gases and alloy heat treatment. Fick's first law for one-dimensional binary diffusion relative to molar average motion is JA=−DAB dcA/dz, with DAB in m²/s. For constant total molar concentration C, JA=−CDAB dyA/dz. The total molar flux NA=JA+yA(NA+NB). In equimolar counterdiffusion NA=−NB, so total molar flow is zero and NA=CDAB(yA1−yA2)/L for steady conditions. In stagnant B, NB=0; solve NA(1−yA)=−CDAB dyA/dz, giving NA=(CDAB/L)ln[(1−yA2)/(1−yA1)]. This includes bulk motion caused by A transfer. In steady laminar flow over a surface the concentration boundary layer develops analogously to the thermal layer.

Solid diffusion can occur through vacancies (substitutional atoms) or interstitial sites (small atoms). Diffusivity often follows D=D0 exp(−Ea/RT), increasing strongly with temperature. Fick's second law for constant D is ∂c/∂t=D∇²c, describing unsteady diffusion. Convective mass transfer NA=kc(cAs−cA∞) defines kc in m/s for concentration driving force. Sherwood Sh=kcL/D, Schmidt Sc=ν/D; for a laminar plate a typical average Sh=0.664 Re^0.5 Sc^1/3 with appropriate assumptions. Overall coefficients combine film resistances; if equilibrium y*=mx and flux is expressed using mole fractions, 1/Ky=1/ky+m/kx. Be consistent about driving forces and coefficient units.

### Worked examples

Equimolar diffusion: D=2×10⁻⁵ m²/s, C=40 mol/m³, L=0.01 m, yA1=0.20, yA2=0.05. NA=40×2×10⁻⁵×0.15/0.01=0.012 mol/m²s. Through stagnant B, NA=0.08 ln(0.95/0.80)=0.01375 mol/m²s. The latter is larger due to bulk motion. For a surface A=0.5 m², kc=0.01 m/s, Δc=0.2 mol/m³, transfer rate=0.001 mol/s. For water (18 g/mol), mass rate=0.018 g/s.

### Exam and lab

Derive equimolar and stagnant-film expressions from Fick's law, state assumptions and compare. Explain solid diffusion and overall coefficients. Cooling tower: record water and air temperatures, humidity and flow rates; estimate evaporation from measured water loss or an air-side humidity balance, distinguish drift and blowdown. Simulate concentration transport and verify grid independence and mass conservation.

## Practical and project supplement

Use instructor-approved setups and actual observations. Heat conduction: compare thermal conductivity of solids/liquids, record geometry and steady temperatures, use Q=kAΔT/L with loss correction. T-history: record cooling/heating curves, compare material response and heat capacity using apparatus method. Convection: determine natural/forced h, examine dimensionless trends; lumped test compare measured cooling curve with exponential model; sensible heat Q=mcΔT, latent heat Q=mhfg. Radiation: estimate emissivity or exchange using calibrated sensors and correct for surroundings. Heat exchangers: compare parallel/counterflow, boiling, agitated vessel and condenser experiments using measured energy balance. IC engine heat balance: input rate=ṁfuel LHV; useful brake power=2πNT/60; cooling-water heat=ṁw cpΔT; exhaust heat from measured mass flow/temperature; remainder is unaccounted loss. Report fractions of fuel energy, not fabricated values. Thermal simulation and cooling tower: use measured or stated boundary conditions, mesh study and validation. Project: choose e.g. insulated container or compact exchanger; define requirement, sketch concept, calculate expected performance, prototype/simulate, compare results, discuss cost, safety and limitations. Deliver design review, intermediate results and final report according to faculty schedule.

# 24MEP403 | Manufacturing Processes

**40-mark ESE | 60-mark CIA | 4 credits | includes laboratory**

## Module 1 — Shaping: casting and polymer processing

### Classification of processes

Manufacturing converts material into useful products. Primary shaping produces a basic geometry by casting, moulding or powder consolidation; deformation changes shape without intentionally removing material; machining removes material; joining combines parts; finishing improves surface; additive manufacturing builds from digital geometry. Selection depends on material, shape, tolerances, batch size, equipment cost, energy and waste. Casting makes complex cavities and large shapes, forming gives good material utilization, machining offers precision, and joining allows assembly of separate materials.

### Metal casting

Sand casting uses a pattern to create a cavity in a disposable sand mould. Pattern allowances include shrinkage, machining, draft and sometimes distortion. The cope is upper mould, drag lower mould; a core creates internal hollows. The gating system has pouring basin, sprue, runner and ingate; a riser feeds liquid metal as the casting shrinks. Steps: prepare pattern, ram mould, withdraw pattern, set core, assemble, pour, solidify, shake out and inspect. Low tooling cost and size flexibility suit small batches; rougher surface and lower accuracy are limits. Die casting forces molten metal into a permanent metal die, yielding fast production and good finish but costly tooling and alloy/size restrictions. Investment casting uses expendable wax patterns coated in ceramic; melt out wax, fire shell, pour and break shell. It produces intricate accurate shapes such as turbine components, but costs more and takes longer.

*Simplified two-part sand mould showing the pouring path and riser; actual gating design depends on geometry. (See PDF for the labelled illustration.)*

### Engineering calculations and defects

Heat needed = m[cs(Tm−Ti) + Lf + cl(Tp−Tm)], ignoring losses; cs/cl are solid/liquid specific heats and Lf latent heat. Bernoulli ideal pouring speed v = √(2gh); continuity Q = Av; filling time = V/Q, assuming steady flow. Actual gating losses reduce flow. Chvorinov's rule ts = Cm(V/A)ⁿ, often n≈2; the riser must solidify after the part and have sufficient feed volume. Casting defects include gas porosity (gas escape), shrinkage cavities (poor feeding), cold shuts and misruns (insufficient fluidity), sand inclusions and hot tears. Use smooth section transitions, fillets, uniform wall thickness, proper vents and directional solidification; avoid unnecessary thick junctions.

Thermoplastics soften again when heated; thermosets cure into crosslinked structures and cannot simply be remelted. Injection moulding plasticizes material in a heated barrel, injects into a closed mould, packs, cools/cures and ejects. High output, complex parts; high mould cost. Blow moulding inflates a hot hollow parison or preform inside a mould, suitable for bottles; wall thickness control is important.

### Worked examples

A 2 kg alloy heats from 25 to 600°C, melts with Lf = 200 kJ/kg and pours at 650°C. cs = 0.5 and cl = 0.6 kJ/kg K. Q = 2[0.5×575+200+0.6×50] = 1,035 kJ. A sprue head 0.2 m gives ideal v = √(2×9.81×0.2)=1.981 m/s. Gate area 200 mm² = 0.0002 m², Q = 0.000396 m³/s; cavity 0.002 m³ fills in 5.05 s ideally. If casting modulus V/A=1 cm and riser modulus=1.3 cm, same mould constant and n=2, riser solidifies 1.69 times as slowly.

### Exam practice

Explain sand casting with labels; compare sand, die and investment methods. Explain why risers need a larger modulus. Calculate ideal fill time using the two equations, and explain why actual time differs.

## Module 2 — Forming and nontraditional machining

### Metal forming

Plastic deformation changes shape permanently. Hot working above recrystallization temperature reduces flow stress and restores grains; cold working improves finish and dimensional accuracy but causes strain hardening and requires larger force. Forging compresses material between dies: open die is flexible, closed die creates a near-net shape. Rolling reduces thickness between rotating rolls. Extrusion pushes material through a die; drawing pulls wire through a die. Shearing cuts sheet; blanking makes the cut piece the product, punching makes a hole. Bending produces an angle with elastic springback. Deep drawing pulls a sheet blank into a die to make cups; a blank holder limits wrinkling. Excessive draw can tear the cup.

For ideal frictionless cylindrical upset forging, constant volume gives A0h0=Ah. True compressive strain magnitude ε=ln(h0/h); instantaneous load F≈YfA, where Yf is current flow stress. A common simplified friction correction for flat dies is F≈Yf A(1+μD/(3h)). Rolling contact length L≈√(RΔh); roll force F≈wL Yavg under a simplified mean-pressure model. Torque per roll ≈ FL/2; power for two rolls ≈2Tω. Maximum draft without external tension is approximately μ²R.

*Flat rolling: rotating rolls reduce strip thickness; material moves from left to right. (See PDF for the labelled illustration.)*

### Nontraditional processes

EDM removes conductive material by pulsed sparks across a dielectric gap; electrodes do not touch workpiece. It machines hard die steels and complex cavities; slow removal and recast layer are disadvantages. Wire EDM continuously feeds a thin electrode wire through a conductive workpiece, producing intricate contours. Abrasive water jet uses high-speed water and abrasives to erode material, works on many materials with little heat affected zone, but has nozzle wear and taper. ECM removes conductive material anodically through an electrolyte; no thermal damage or cutting tool wear, but electrolyte handling and stray machining matter. Faraday law: mass removal rate = ηIM/(zF), M molar mass, z valence, F≈96,485 C/mol. Divide by density for volume rate and frontal area for feed speed. Ultrasonic machining uses a vibrating tool and abrasive slurry to erode hard brittle material; low thermal damage, slow rate. Electron beam machining uses focused electrons in vacuum for fine holes; laser beam machining uses focused light, both thermal processes with possible heat affected zone. Plasma arc uses ionized gas for rapid cutting of conducting metals, with lower precision and thermal effects compared with fine laser processes.

### Worked examples

Roll radius 250 mm, thickness drop 2 mm, strip width 100 mm, mean pressure 150 MPa. L≈√500=22.36 mm. F≈100×22.36×150=335.4 kN. Torque per roll ≈3,750 N·m; at 60 rpm, two-roll power ≈47.1 kW. For iron ECM, I=100 A, M=55.85 g/mol, z=2, η=1, mass rate=0.02894 g/s; density 7.87 g/cm³ gives 0.00368 cm³/s. Real valence and current efficiency depend on process chemistry.

### Exam practice

Compare EDM, ECM, USM and abrasive water jet by energy source, suitable materials, advantages and limitations. Explain forging/rolling/extrusion/drawing with sketches. Draw deep drawing with punch, die and blank holder. Calculate rolling force and power using provided process data.

## Module 3 — Machining, tools and machining economics

### Conventional cutting operations

Turning rotates the workpiece and feeds a single-point tool; facing makes a flat end, taper turning changes diameter. Drilling rotates a multi-edge drill to produce a hole; reaming improves its size and finish. Milling uses a rotating multi-tooth cutter; peripheral milling cuts with the circumference, face milling with end and peripheral edges. Up milling feeds opposite local cutting direction, down milling feeds with it and needs backlash control. Grinding uses abrasive grains to achieve fine finish and accurate dimensions; honing improves bore geometry, lapping improves precision surface, polishing reduces visible roughness.

For turning with D in mm, N rpm, feed f mm/rev, depth d mm: cutting speed V=πDN/1000 m/min, feed speed=fN, time=L/(fN) min, approximate MRR=πDNfd mm³/min for small d (use mean diameter for exact annular area). Drilling MRR=πD²fN/4. Milling table feed=fz zN where fz is feed per tooth, z teeth; MRR=width×depth×table feed. Add approach and overtravel to actual cutting length. Cost includes machine time, tool use and handling.

*Schematic turning operation: a single-point tool moves axially along a rotating workpiece. (See PDF for the labelled illustration.)*

### Cutting tools and chip mechanics

Single point tool ASA signature lists back rake, side rake, end relief, side relief, end cutting-edge angle, side cutting-edge angle and nose radius. Rake affects cutting force and chip flow; relief avoids rubbing; nose radius affects finish and strength. HSS is tough and economical at low speed, carbide permits higher speed, ceramics handle high temperatures but may be brittle, CBN suits hardened steels, diamond suits many nonferrous/abrasive materials but reacts with iron at high cutting temperatures. Cutting fluids cool, lubricate, flush chips and reduce corrosion; select for material, environmental and safety needs. Machinability describes ease of obtaining required removal rate, finish, tool life and low force. Continuous chips form commonly in ductile materials, built-up edge at certain speeds and friction, discontinuous chips in brittle materials, segmented chips in some high-speed alloys.

In orthogonal cutting, chip ratio r=t1/t2 and shear angle tan φ=r cos α/(1−r sin α). With cutting force Fc and thrust Ft: friction F=Fc sin α+Ft cos α; normal on rake N=Fc cos α−Ft sin α; shear force Fs=Fc cos φ−Ft sin φ. Cutting power≈FcV. Tool wear includes flank, crater and notch wear; failure also occurs through chipping. Taylor equation VTⁿ=C, where T is tool life in minutes, n and C experimental constants. Higher speed raises productivity but decreases tool life; balance tool-change time, insert cost and machine rate.

### Worked examples

Turning D=60 mm, N=500 rpm, f=0.2 mm/rev, d=2 mm, travel 100 mm. V=94.25 m/min, time=1 min, MRR≈37,699 mm³/min. For drilling D=10 mm at N=800, f=0.1, depth travel 30 mm, time=0.375 min and MRR=6,283 mm³/min. For Taylor n=0.25, V=100 m/min at T=60 min, C=100×60^0.25; at V=150, T2=60(100/150)^4=11.85 min. At Fc=500 N and speed 120 m/min=2 m/s, cutting power=1 kW.

### Exam practice

Draw a labelled lathe cutting tool; explain chip forms, tool materials, grinding and machining economics. Solve a cutting time/MRR problem; for milling fz=0.1, z=4, N=500, answer feed 200 mm/min. For simulation, vary speed/feed and plot measured or calculated force with assumptions.

## Module 4 — Joining and fastening

### Welding principles and joints

Joining makes assemblies; removable mechanical fasteners (nuts, bolts) differ from permanent joints. Welding joins by heat, pressure or both. Fusion welding melts base material; solid-state welding joins without bulk melting. Joint geometries include butt, lap, tee, corner and edge; fillet and groove describe weld shape. Arc welding converts electrical energy to heat: electric power VI, heat reaching workpiece ≈ηVI, line heat input H=ηVI/v with travel speed v in mm/s gives J/mm.

SMAW uses a flux-coated consumable stick electrode; flux produces shielding and slag. Simple portable equipment suits site work but electrode changes and slag removal slow production. GMAW (MIG/MAG) continuously feeds a consumable wire with shielding gas; high productivity, often automated, but wind disrupts shielding. GTAW (TIG) uses a nonconsumable tungsten electrode and inert shielding gas; separate filler optional. High quality and precision for thin materials, but slower and operator skill needed. Solid-state methods include friction welding (relative motion and pressure), friction stir (rotating tool plasticizes material), diffusion bonding (time, temperature and pressure), ultrasonic welding (vibration). They avoid bulk melting but need process-specific geometry/equipment.

Brazing and soldering melt filler without melting the base, using capillary flow; brazing filler liquidus above 450°C, soldering below or at 450°C by conventional definition. Adhesive bonding joins surfaces by a cured adhesive; surface prep and joint geometry are important, lap joints reduce peel. Weld defects include porosity, lack of fusion/penetration, cracks, undercut, slag inclusion and distortion. Visual inspection detects visible surface problems; liquid penetrant finds open surface defects; magnetic particle inspection finds surface/near-surface defects in ferromagnetic materials; ultrasonic and radiography can detect internal defects. Destructive tensile/bend tests evaluate strength and ductility. Design with access, suitable joint preparation, balanced weld sequence, fatigue-sensitive geometry and inspection requirements.

### Worked example

Arc voltage 25 V, current 180 A, efficiency 0.8, travel speed 5 mm/s. Power = 25×180=4,500 W; net heat rate = 3,600 W; heat input = 720 J/mm = 0.72 kJ/mm. A 200 mm joint takes 40 s of arc time and receives 144 kJ. Actual energy includes setup losses. For comparison of welding parameters, hold material and geometry constant and vary current or speed separately; measure bead width, penetration and defects with approved lab procedures.

### Exam practice

Compare SMAW, MIG and TIG with electrode, shielding, advantages and industrial applications. Explain brazing versus soldering versus welding. Explain inspection method selection for a surface crack and an internal lack of fusion. Draw five joint configurations and label a fillet weld.

## Module 5 — Powder metallurgy and additive manufacturing

### Powder processing

Powder metallurgy makes components from metal powder. Sequence: powder production, blending with additives/lubricant, compaction into a green compact, sintering below the main constituent melting temperature (liquid-phase sintering may use a liquid), sizing or finishing. Diffusion bonds particles and improves strength. Benefits: near-net shape, controlled porosity, high production, little scrap; limits: expensive powder/dies, size and density gradients, residual pores. Applications include self-lubricating bearings, filters, gears and hard-metal tools.

### Layer-by-layer manufacture

Additive manufacturing builds a part directly from digital geometry. Workflow: CAD → export suitable mesh or model → check geometry → choose orientation/support → slice → build → remove supports and postprocess → inspect. Material extrusion (FDM/FFF) extrudes softened filament, affordable but anisotropy and visible layers; vat photopolymerization cures liquid resin with light, excellent detail but material limits and cleaning/curing; powder bed fusion selectively fuses powder with laser or electron beam, complex strong parts but high equipment cost, residual stress and powder safety; directed energy deposition feeds powder/wire into a melt pool, useful for repair and larger deposits, lower precision; binder jetting deposits binder into powder then cures or sinters, faster printing but shrinkage/porosity; sheet lamination bonds and cuts sheets, fast for some materials but limited internal features. Material jetting deposits droplets and cures them, good detail and multi-material models but expensive feedstock.

Defects include lack of fusion, voids, warping, delamination, dimensional error and rough surfaces. Orientation affects anisotropy, supports and time; thin walls, overhangs and trapped powder require design attention. Post-processing may include machining, heat treatment or inspection. Compare AM with casting/machining using lifecycle cost, batch size and strength rather than assuming AM is always superior.

### Worked example — Cycle time and cost

A printed part has height 40 mm and layer height 0.2 mm: 200 layers. If estimated deposition time per layer is 12 s and overhead 3 s, build time=3,000 s=50 min, excluding setup and postprocessing. Material 80 g at ₹2/g gives ₹160. Machine rate ₹240/h for 50 min costs ₹200. Add setup/postprocess ₹100 gives estimated cost ₹460. Change orientation to reduce layer count only if support and surface requirements remain acceptable.

### Exam practice

Explain powder metallurgy with a flow chart; compare FDM, vat polymerization, powder bed fusion and binder jetting. Explain how orientation affects build quality and cost. Calculate time from layer height and average layer time. Discuss three print defects and their likely causes.
