Follow the instructor's operating procedures, machine guards and PPE. Never perform casting, welding or powered machining without authorized supervision. Record actual values, units and observations; no invented lab readings.

1. Sand mould/casting: record pattern dimensions, allowances, sand type and mould features; compare actual part dimensions; for sand tests record specimen size and peak load, strength=load/area with test-specific geometry.

# 24MET401 | Mechanics of Deformable Solids

**60-mark ESE | 40-mark CIA | 4 credits**

## Module 1 — Stress and strain at a point

### Why we study this

A beam in a building, a shaft in a motor and a rod in a machine all deform when forces act on them. A rigid-body analysis gives reactions and forces but cannot tell us how much a component stretches or whether it will fail. Mechanics of deformable solids connects external loads, internal stresses and deformation.

### Internal forces and stress

Cut an imaginary section through a body in equilibrium. Draw the free-body diagram of one part and apply the three force and moment equilibrium equations as required. The internal force on the cut balances the external forces. Normal stress acts perpendicular to the section; shear stress acts parallel to it. The average direct stress is force divided by cross-sectional area. Tensile stress is taken positive and compression negative. Stress has units N/mm² = MPa.

At a point, stress depends on the orientation of the cut. The stress tensor is a 3 × 3 matrix with normal stresses on the diagonal and shear components off the diagonal. Moment equilibrium of a small element gives equality of complementary shear stresses, such as τxy = τyx, in classical continuum mechanics. Consequently six independent stress components describe the general symmetric tensor.

### Traction, displacement and strain

Cauchy's equation is t = σn, where n is a unit normal and σ is the stress tensor. The normal stress on the plane is n·t; the shear traction vector is t − (n·t)n. Its magnitude is the length of this vector. This is a general method to find stress on any plane.

Displacement describes the movement of a material point, with components u, v and w along x, y and z. For small deformation, εx = ∂u/∂x, εy = ∂v/∂y and εz = ∂w/∂z. Engineering shear strain γxy = ∂u/∂y + ∂v/∂x. The tensor shear strain is half the engineering shear strain. In compact form ε = ½(grad u + grad uᵀ). The antisymmetric part represents infinitesimal rotation, not strain.

Plane stress is a good model of a thin plate loaded in its plane: σz = τxz = τyz = 0, but εz may be nonzero. Plane strain is used for a long constrained body: εz = γxz = γyz = 0, but σz may be nonzero.

### Principal stresses and Mohr's circle

Principal planes carry normal stress without shear. Their normals are eigenvectors of σ; the corresponding eigenvalues are principal stresses. The three stress invariants are unchanged by a change of coordinate axes: I1 = tr(σ), I2 = sum of the three principal-stress pair products, I3 = det(σ). Find eigenvalues by solving det(σ − λI) = 0 or using a symmetric-matrix eigenvalue function in software.

For plane stress, define C = (σx + σy)/2 and R = √[((σx − σy)/2)² + τxy²]. Then σ1,2 = C ± R. The maximum in-plane shear is R; the absolute maximum shear is (largest − smallest of σ1, σ2, 0)/2. The principal angle obeys tan(2θp) = 2τxy/(σx − σy), with quadrant chosen using atan2. On Mohr's circle plot the points (σx, τxy) and (σy, −τxy); the centre lies on the normal-stress axis. A physical rotation of θ corresponds to 2θ on the circle; follow the chosen shear sign convention consistently.

*Mohr circle for the worked example, with positive shear plotted upward. Horizontal scale is schematic. (See PDF for the labelled illustration.)*

### Worked problem 1 — Principal stresses

Given σx = 80 MPa, σy = 20 MPa and τxy = 40 MPa. C = 50 MPa. R = √(30² + 40²) = 50 MPa. Therefore the two principal stresses are 100 MPa and 0 MPa. θp = ½ atan2(80, 60) = 26.565°. The absolute maximum shear is 50 MPa. Check: the sum of principal stresses is 100 MPa, equal to σx + σy.

### Worked problem 2 — Strain matrix

Given u = 0.002x + 0.003y, v = −0.001x + 0.001y and w = 0 (consistent length units). εx = 0.002, εy = 0.001, γxy = 0.003 − 0.001 = 0.002. The in-plane strain tensor has diagonal entries 0.002 and 0.001 and off-diagonal entries 0.001. Strain has no units.

### Exam practice with answers

Define principal plane. Answer: a plane on which the traction has no tangential component. Differentiate plane stress and plane strain using the conditions above. For a long answer, derive the traction relation and draw Mohr's circle, identify centre, radius, principal stresses and maximum shear. Practice: σx = 60, σy = 20, τxy = 0 MPa. Answer: principal stresses 60 and 20 MPa, maximum in-plane shear 20 MPa and absolute maximum shear 30 MPa.

## Module 2 — Elasticity and axial members

### Stress–strain behaviour

In a tensile test, a specimen is pulled gradually. Engineering stress is P/A0 and engineering strain is extension divided by original gauge length. A ductile metal such as mild steel shows elastic behaviour, yielding, plastic deformation, strain hardening, ultimate tensile stress and necking before fracture. A brittle material fractures with little plastic deformation. Young's modulus E is the slope of the initial linear region. The 0.2% offset proof stress is used for materials without a clear yield point. Poisson's ratio ν is minus lateral strain divided by axial strain under uniaxial loading.

*Qualitative engineering stress-strain curves of a ductile material (teal) and a brittle material (red); not test data. (See PDF for the labelled illustration.)*

### Hooke's law in three dimensions

For linear isotropic elasticity, εx = [σx − ν(σy + σz)]/E; cyclic permutation gives εy and εz. Add αΔT to each normal strain if free thermal expansion is included. Shear follows γxy = τxy/G. Here G is shear modulus, K is bulk modulus, α is coefficient of linear thermal expansion and ΔT is temperature change. E = 2G(1 + ν) = 3K(1 − 2ν). Plane stress: set σz = 0 in these equations. Plane strain: set εz = 0 and solve for σz; without heating, σz = ν(σx + σy). The distinction is essential when deciding stiffness and stress.

### Axial deformation and compatibility

From σ = P/A and ε = δ/L = σ/E, obtain δ = PL/(AE). This applies to a uniform bar with constant axial load and linear elastic material. For stepped bars use δ = Σ(PiLi/AiEi), retaining the sign of each force. For a varying area or load use integration of N(x)/(A(x)E(x)) over length. Equilibrium alone is insufficient for a statically indeterminate structure; add deformation compatibility and material equations. For parallel bars between rigid plates, extension is equal and the total force is the sum of bar forces. For a fixed-ended bar, total change in length is zero.

A freely heated bar expands by δT = αLΔT with no stress. If fully prevented from expanding, thermal stress is −EαΔT for heating. Partial restraint needs a compatibility equation, not the full-restraint formula.

### Worked problem 1 — Stepped rod

A 20 kN tensile force acts on a steel rod made of a 400 mm segment with area 200 mm² and a 600 mm segment with area 300 mm². E = 200,000 MPa. Stresses are 100 and 66.67 MPa. Extension = (20,000 × 400)/(200 × 200,000) + (20,000 × 600)/(300 × 200,000) = 0.20 + 0.20 = 0.40 mm.

### Worked problem 2 — Fully restrained heating

A steel bar has E = 200 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ /K and is heated by 50 K. Free strain would be 0.0006. Because the ends cannot move, elastic strain is −0.0006, giving σ = −120 MPa. If A = 250 mm², the reaction magnitude is 30 kN.

### Worked problem 3 — Parallel bars

Two equal-length rods (steel E = 200 GPa, aluminium E = 70 GPa), each of area 100 mm², support a 27 kN load through rigid plates. The common strain is 27,000/(20,000,000 + 7,000,000) = 0.001. Steel stress = 200 MPa and aluminium stress = 70 MPa. Forces are 20 and 7 kN, satisfying equilibrium.

### Exam practice with answers

Explain the ductile stress–strain curve; label yield, ultimate strength and fracture. Derive the relation E = 2G(1 + ν) by applying pure shear and evaluating the principal strains. Short question: why does a free heated bar have no stress? Answer: no constraint opposes its expansion. Practice: a 1 m rod, area 500 mm², E = 200 GPa under 50 kN has extension 0.5 mm.

## Module 3 — Torsion, shear force and bending moment

### Circular shaft under torque

Torque is the twisting moment about the shaft axis. In an elastic circular shaft, cross sections remain plane and rotate relative to one another; radial lines remain straight and the angle of twist varies along the shaft. Assume a homogeneous isotropic material, small deformation, circular section and elastic stresses. A fibre at radius r experiences γ = rθ/L, so τ = Grθ/L. Integrating the moment of the shear stress over the cross section gives T = (Gθ/L)∫r²dA = GJθ/L. Hence T/J = τ/r = Gθ/L. J = πd⁴/32 for a solid shaft; J = π(Do⁴ − Di⁴)/32 for a hollow shaft. GJ is torsional rigidity. Power transmitted is P = 2πNT/60 with N in rpm and torque in N·m. Design a shaft for both allowable shear stress and allowable twist, then adopt the larger required diameter.

### Shear force and bending moment

A beam is a member loaded mainly transverse to its length. Shear force V is the algebraic sum of transverse forces on one side of an imaginary cut; bending moment M is the internal moment needed for equilibrium. Begin with a free-body diagram and calculate support reactions. Choose upward load reaction positive and sagging moment positive. With downward distributed load w positive, dV/dx = −w and dM/dx = V. A concentrated force causes a jump in V; an applied concentrated couple causes a jump in M. With no distributed load, V is constant and M linear; with uniform load, V varies linearly and M quadratically. A point of zero shear is a candidate location of maximum or minimum moment. At a simple support without applied end couple, M = 0. At a free end without end load/couple, both V and M are zero.

*Simply supported beam under a full-span UDL; upward reactions and downward load are shown. (See PDF for the labelled illustration.)*

### Worked problem 1 — Shaft design

A solid shaft carries 500 N·m, with allowable shear 50 MPa. Convert T = 500,000 N·mm. Using τmax = 16T/(πd³), d³ = 16 × 500,000/(π × 50) = 50,930 mm³, so d = 37.07 mm. Choose at least 38 mm for strength alone. The twist and fatigue checks may require a larger diameter. For d = 40 mm, L = 1,000 mm and G = 80,000 MPa, J = 251,327 mm⁴, θ = TL/GJ = 0.02487 rad = 1.425°.

### Worked problem 2 — Simply supported beam

A 6 m beam carries 4 kN/m over its whole span. Total load = 24 kN, so RA = RB = 12 kN. At distance x from A, V = 12 − 4x kN and M = 12x − 2x² kN·m. At x = 3 m, V = 0 and M = 18 kN·m, the maximum sagging moment. Draw a straight shear line from +12 to −12 and a parabolic moment curve from zero to 18 and back to zero.

### Worked problem 3 — Cantilever

A 2 m cantilever with 5 kN downward tip force has fixed-end vertical reaction 5 kN and reaction moment 10 kN·m. From the fixed end, V is constant (+5 kN with the adopted convention) and internal M = −5(2 − x) kN·m. The bending moment diagram is triangular, hogging at the support and zero at the free tip.

### Computational exercise and exam practice

Create a table of x, V and M in a spreadsheet and plot the curves; include points immediately before and after concentrated loads. Confirm the moment diagram derivative matches shear. Explain the assumptions of torsion and derive its equation. For a 4 m simply supported beam with 10 kN at midspan, answer: 5 kN reactions, maximum moment 10 kN·m.

## Module 4 — Bending stress and beam deflection

### Flexure theory

Bending makes the fibres on one side of the neutral surface stretch and the other side shorten. For a homogeneous, prismatic, elastic beam under small curvature, plane sections remain plane. At distance y from the neutral axis, strain magnitude is y/R, where R is radius of curvature. Hooke's law gives σ = Ey/R (sign from tension/compression). The zero net axial force condition puts the neutral axis at the centroid for pure bending of a homogeneous section. Integrating σy over area yields M = EI/R. Thus M/I = σ/y = E/R in magnitude. I is the second moment of area about the neutral axis; Z = I/ymax is section modulus, and EI is flexural rigidity. Maximum stress is M/Z. A rectangular section has I = bh³/12 and Z = bh²/6; a solid circular section has I = πd⁴/64. I-sections are efficient because much of their material is far from the neutral axis.

### Transverse shear stress

The formula τ = VQ/(Ib) gives the shear stress at a level where b is local section width and Q is first moment of the area above or below that level about the neutral axis. It follows from the longitudinal change in bending force over a short length. For a rectangular section, τ(y) = (3V/2A)[1 − (2y/h)²]. The maximum is 1.5V/A at the neutral axis; it vanishes at the top and bottom free surfaces. The web of an I-beam carries much of the shear.

### Slope and deflection

For small slopes, EI d²v/dx² = M(x), using upward deflection v and sagging-positive moment. Integrate once for slope and again for deflection; determine constants from boundary conditions. At a fixed end both v and dv/dx are zero; at a pin/roller v = 0. Macaulay brackets <x−a>ⁿ are zero for x < a and (x−a)ⁿ otherwise, allowing several concentrated loads and UDLs to be expressed in a single equation. For a UDL beginning at a and ending at b, the moment terms are −w<x−a>²/2 + w<x−b>²/2. Integrate bracket powers in the usual way. At changes of EI use separate regions and enforce displacement and slope continuity.

### Worked problem 1 — Bending and shear

A rectangular beam b = 100 mm, h = 200 mm has M = 20 kN·m and V = 15 kN. Z = 100 × 200²/6 = 666,667 mm³. σmax = 20,000,000/666,667 = 30 MPa. A = 20,000 mm²; τmax = 1.5 × 15,000/20,000 = 1.125 MPa. The stress maxima occur at different levels.

### Worked problem 2 — Double integration

A simply supported beam of span L carries a central point force P. On the left half, M = Px/2. Integrate: EI v′ = Px²/4 + C1 and EI v = Px³/12 + C1x + C2. At x = 0, v = 0 gives C2 = 0; at x = L/2, symmetry gives v′ = 0, so C1 = −PL²/16. Midspan downward deflection magnitude is PL³/(48EI). For P = 10,000 N, L = 2,000 mm, E = 200,000 MPa, I = 8 × 10⁶ mm⁴, it is 1.042 mm.

### Worked problem 3 — Macaulay equation

For a span 4 m with central load 8 kN and full UDL 2 kN/m, reactions are 8 kN each. M = 8x − x² − 8<x−2> (kN·m). EI v = (8/6)x³ − x⁴/12 − (8/6)<x−2>³ + C1x + C2. Set v(0)=v(4)=0: C2=0, C1=−13.333 kN·m². At x=2, EI v = −17.333 kN·m³. Divide by EI in kN·m² to obtain deflection in m. Check symmetry: v′(2)=0.

### Exam practice

Derive flexural and shear stress formulas, sketch their distributions and compare I- and rectangular sections. For beam selection, calculate Zrequired = Mmax/σallow and Irequired from the deflection limit. Verify shear and stability separately.

## Module 5 — Buckling and combined loading

### Stability of columns

A short compression member usually fails through material crushing or yielding. A slender column can suddenly bow sideways at a smaller load: buckling. For a perfect column with a small lateral deflection, equilibrium gives EI y″ + Py = 0. For pinned ends y(0) = y(L) = 0. The first nonzero solution occurs when √(P/EI)L = π; therefore Pcr = π²EI/L². Higher mathematical modes need larger loads. The straight equilibrium path bifurcates into a buckled path at the ideal critical load. Real columns have imperfections and do not exhibit a perfectly sharp bifurcation.

For other ideal support conditions use effective length Le: pinned–pinned L; fixed–free 2L; fixed–fixed L/2; fixed–pinned approximately 0.7L. Choose the weak bending axis (smallest I). Radius of gyration k = √(I/A), slenderness ratio λ = Le/k, critical stress σcr = π²E/λ². Euler theory assumes a long, straight, elastic, centrally loaded member. Rankine's empirical formula combines crushing and buckling: P = σc A/[1 + a(Le/k)²], where σc and a are material-dependent constants. Do not use an arbitrary value of a without data. A design load must also allow for safety, imperfections and applicable codes.

*Idealized column end conditions and qualitative first buckling shapes; effective length Le is listed. (See PDF for the labelled illustration.)*

### Combined loading

A member may be loaded by an axial force P, bending M and torsion T at the same time. Under linear elasticity, superpose normal stresses: σ = P/A ± My/I at the selected point. Torsional shear in a circular shaft is τ = Tr/J. If transverse shear also matters, combine shear components with their directions. Apply the stress transformation formulas of Module 1 to compute principal stresses. For a ductile material, the plane-stress von Mises equivalent stress is √(σx² − σxσy + σy² + 3τxy²). Check an appropriate failure criterion and allowable value. Superposition applies only if the response remains linear.

### Worked problem 1 — Euler load

A pinned steel column has L = 2,000 mm, E = 200,000 MPa, Imin = 2 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Pcr = π² × 200,000 × 2 × 10⁶/2,000² = 986,960 N = 987 kN. If fixed–free instead, Le doubles and the load is one quarter, 247 kN. Check whether the computed stress stays within the elastic range before using this result.

### Worked problem 2 — Rankine load

For A = 1,000 mm², σc = 300 MPa, a = 1/7,500, Le/k = 100, P = 300,000/(1 + 10,000/7,500) = 128.57 kN. With factor of safety 3 the illustrative allowable load is 42.86 kN.

### Worked problem 3 — Combined stress

At a shaft surface the combined axial and bending normal stress is 80 MPa and torsional shear is 30 MPa. The other in-plane normal stress is zero. C = 40 MPa, R = √(40² + 30²) = 50 MPa. Principal stresses are 90 and −10 MPa; the third is zero. Absolute maximum shear = 50 MPa. Von Mises stress = √(80² + 3 × 30²) = 95.39 MPa.

### Case study and exam practice

Analyse a bicycle seat post or machine support column: draw loads, identify end restraints, compute axial and bending stress, assess buckling, state assumptions and propose a safer section. Exam question: derive Euler's load for pinned ends and compare all four end conditions. Short answer: a fixed–fixed column's ideal critical load is four times that of a pinned column of the same physical length.

## Module 1 — Measurement fundamentals and instruments

### Measurement quality

Metrology is the science of measurement. It is needed because a machine assembled from separately manufactured parts works only when the parts meet their specified dimensions and quality requirements. A measurement compares an unknown quantity with a reference. A result should include value, unit and uncertainty. Traceability means an unbroken documented calibration chain to a recognized reference, with stated uncertainty at each step.

Accuracy is closeness to a reference value; precision is closeness of repeated readings. Resolution is the smallest change that can be distinguished; range is the interval of measurable values. Sensitivity is output change per input change. Repeatability is precision under the same conditions, reproducibility under changed conditions. Systematic error creates bias (zero offset, scale error, temperature effect); random error causes scatter. Gross errors such as transcription mistakes must be investigated. Error is measured value minus reference value; correction is its negative. Uncertainty estimates the spread of plausible values and is not identical to error. Calibration compares readings against standards to establish their relationship; adjustment is a separate action.

Abbe's principle says the measurement axis should be collinear with the dimension being measured. A small angular error θ with an offset h creates approximately hθ error. For h = 50 mm and θ = 0.001 rad, error is 0.05 mm. Reduce offset or use aligned instruments. Control temperature; metal parts change size by αLΔT.

### Linear and angular measurement

Vernier caliper: main scale, sliding vernier, outside and inside jaws, depth rod. Least count is one main-scale division minus one vernier division for a direct vernier. Reading = main-scale reading + coinciding vernier division × least count − signed zero error. Micrometer uses a screw: least count = pitch / thimble divisions. Use the ratchet, clean the anvils and avoid excessive force. Slip gauges are precision length blocks which can be wrung together to make a required length. Select the minimum practical combination and handle with clean hands or gloves. Angle gauges work similarly by adding or subtracting standard angles. A sine bar rests on two accurately spaced rollers, one on a gauge-block stack: sin θ = h/L. The bevel protractor reads angles directly. An Angle Dekkor is an optical small-angle comparison instrument; a clinometer measures inclination relative to gravity.

Comparators indicate deviation from a reference rather than absolute dimension: mechanical uses levers/gears, electrical converts displacement to signal, optical magnifies angular movement with light, and pneumatic senses clearance through air pressure or flow. Set zero with a master before measuring. Pneumatic gauges are useful for repetitive bore measurement.

*Sine bar: roller centres are separated by L, one roller is raised by h; sin(theta) = h/L. (See PDF for the labelled illustration.)*

### Worked examples

Vernier: main scale 22 mm, coincidence 7, least count 0.02 mm, positive zero error 0.04 mm. Result = 22 + 0.14 − 0.04 = 22.10 mm. Micrometer: pitch 0.5 mm, 50 divisions, sleeve 8.5 mm, thimble 28; reading = 8.5 + 0.28 = 8.78 mm before correction. Sine bar: L = 200 mm, angle 30°; gauge stack height = 200 sin 30° = 100 mm. Combined independent standard uncertainties 0.03 and 0.04 mm yield √(0.03²+0.04²) = 0.05 mm; state assumptions before combining.

### Exam practice

Explain calibration versus adjustment and accuracy versus precision. Draw a sine bar and derive sin θ = h/L. Compare four comparator types by operating principle, advantages and limits. Practice: pitch 0.5 mm, 100 divisions; answer least count 0.005 mm.

## Module 2 — Limits, fits, gauges and GD&T

### Size limits and fit

Manufacturing cannot produce every part at exactly its nominal size. The basic size is the design reference; upper and lower deviations specify permissible departures. Maximum limit minus minimum limit is tolerance. Fundamental deviation locates the tolerance zone relative to the zero line; IT grade sets its width for a given size range. A hole-basis system holds the hole lower deviation at zero (H), and varies the shaft zone; a shaft-basis system holds the shaft upper deviation at zero (h). Clearance fit always allows a gap; interference fit always requires overlap; transition fit can produce either. Maximum clearance = largest hole − smallest shaft; minimum clearance = smallest hole − largest shaft. Negative clearance means interference.

*Schematic hole-basis tolerance zones, not to scale. A transition fit may have clearance or interference. (See PDF for the labelled illustration.)*

### Limit gauges

A GO gauge checks the maximum-material condition (smallest hole, largest shaft); a NO-GO gauge checks the opposite size limit. Taylor's principle: GO should check related dimensions together in full form; NO-GO should check individual dimensions independently where possible. A plug gauge checks a hole, ring gauge an external cylinder, snap gauge an external width, position gauge the location of a feature; feeler gauge measures a gap using thin blades. Gauge manufacturing tolerance and wear allowance must be assigned using the applicable gauge standard; actual working gauge dimensions are not automatically identical to the ideal workpiece limits.

### Geometric dimensioning and tolerancing

Size alone does not ensure function. Straightness, flatness, circularity and cylindricity control form; parallelism, perpendicularity and angularity control orientation; position controls location; runout controls variation during rotation; profile controls surface or line shape. A datum is a theoretically exact reference established from datum features. A feature-control frame states characteristic, tolerance-zone size/shape and datum references where required. For a circular hole with position tolerance Ø0.10 mm, the axis must lie inside the specified cylindrical zone, subject to the specified datum system and modifiers. Maximum material condition (MMC) means most material (largest shaft or smallest hole); bonus tolerance may apply if MMC is specified. Use the appropriate ISO or ASME standard, not a mixture of conventions. Design for manufacture selects the loosest tolerances that preserve function and specifies accessible measurement methods.

### Worked examples

Hole 25.000–25.025 mm and shaft 24.975–24.990 mm: hole tolerance 0.025 mm, shaft tolerance 0.015 mm. Minimum clearance = 25.000 − 24.990 = 0.010 mm; maximum = 25.025 − 24.975 = 0.050 mm. This is a clearance fit. Ideal GO plug 25.000 mm and NO-GO plug 25.025 mm, ignoring gauge tolerance. Ideal GO ring 24.990 mm and NO-GO ring 24.975 mm. For two dimensions in a stack, 20 ±0.10 and 30 ±0.15 mm, total 50 ±0.25 mm by worst-case addition; RSS uncertainty 0.180 mm if independent values are compatible statistical measures. A hole axis displaced 0.03 mm in x and 0.04 mm in y has diametrical position error 2√(0.03²+0.04²)=0.10 mm.

### Exam practice

Draw tolerance zones for clearance, transition and interference fits; explain Taylor's principle with GO/NO-GO sketches. Distinguish datum from datum feature. Practice: hole 20.00–20.02, shaft 20.03–20.05 mm; answer interference from 0.01 to 0.05 mm.

## Module 3 — Form, surface and optical metrology

### Measuring geometrical form

Straightness is departure from an ideal straight line, flatness from two enclosing parallel planes, and roundness from two enclosing concentric circles in a section. Use a straightedge and indicator, precision surface plate and height indicator, or a roundness tester respectively. Record measured points, select the reference and evaluate error with a stated fitting method (least squares, minimum zone, etc.). Do not confuse datum orientation error with form error. A coordinate measuring machine (CMM) measures x, y, z using a probe; calibration, datum alignment, probe radius compensation and sampling strategy affect results. Optical 3D scanning obtains a dense point cloud; reflective surfaces and occlusion can reduce accuracy. An autocollimator uses a collimated beam reflected from a mirror; return beam angle changes by twice the mirror angle. Move a mirror on a base along a machine surface, measure successive tilts, convert to height changes and reconstruct the profile.

### Optical interference and surface texture

Interference occurs when coherent waves combine. In a Michelson-type instrument, moving one mirror by d changes round-trip path by 2d. Each fringe corresponds to d = λ/2. This gives a traceable way of measuring tiny displacement or calibrating standards. Surface texture includes roughness (small irregularities), waviness (longer variations) and lay (dominant direction). A stylus profiler moves over the surface, records a profile and filters it according to the chosen standard. Ra = mean absolute deviation of the roughness profile; Rq = root mean square deviation; Rt = total peak-to-valley height across evaluation length; Rz is a peak-to-valley parameter defined by the applicable standard (often averaged over sampling lengths). Always specify filter, evaluation length and standard.

Optical microscopes use visible light and lenses; laser scanning microscopes can resolve topography through optical sectioning; SEM uses an electron beam to image fine surface detail, generally requiring vacuum and appropriate sample preparation. Raman spectroscopy detects molecular vibrational signatures from shifted scattered light, useful for identifying materials and sometimes residual stress with calibration; it is not a direct dimensional gauge.

### Worked examples

For equally spaced roughness profile heights −2, +1, −1, +2 µm about the mean: Ra = (2+1+1+2)/4 = 1.5 µm; Rq = √(10/4) = 1.581 µm; Rt = 2 − (−2) = 4 µm. For laser wavelength 632.8 nm, 100 fringes indicate mirror displacement 100 × 632.8/2 nm = 31.64 µm. For autocollimator mirror tilt 20 arcseconds, convert θ = 20π/(180×3600) rad; over a 100 mm base, height difference ≈ 0.00970 mm.

### Exam practice

Explain CMM operation, autocollimator flatness measurement and the principle of interferometry. Draw a roughness profile and label Ra/Rt. Compare optical microscopy, SEM and Raman by measured property and application.

## Module 4 — Transducers, data acquisition, thermal and flow measurements

### Converting physical quantities into signals

A transducer converts a physical quantity into another usable form. Active sensors generate a signal without external excitation (thermocouple); passive sensors require excitation (resistance strain gauge, RTD, LVDT). Important properties are sensitivity, linearity, hysteresis, drift, response time and bandwidth. A bonded strain gauge changes resistance when stretched: gauge factor GF = (ΔR/R)/ε. A Wheatstone bridge converts small resistance variations into voltage. For a quarter bridge with small strain, output magnitude ≈ Vex GF ε/4. Half and full bridges can improve sensitivity and compensate temperature with proper arrangement.

An LVDT uses an AC-excited primary winding, two series-opposed secondary windings and a movable magnetic core. At the central position secondary voltages cancel. Moving the core changes magnitude and phase, indicating displacement and direction. It has no sliding electrical contact. An instrumentation amplifier gives high differential gain and common-mode rejection; an isolation amplifier electrically separates circuits for protection and noise control. A data acquisition chain is sensor → excitation/conditioning → anti-alias filter → ADC → computer → display or control. Sample above twice the maximum signal frequency, with practical margin and filtering.

*LVDT schematic: differential secondary output changes with core displacement. Null is the centred position. (See PDF for the labelled illustration.)*

### Temperature and flow instruments

A thermocouple produces voltage related to temperature difference (Seebeck effect); it needs reference-junction compensation. An RTD measures predictable resistance change, often platinum; R ≈ R0(1+αT) over a limited range. A thermistor is highly sensitive but nonlinear; a pyrometer estimates temperature from emitted radiation, affected by emissivity and optical path. Obstruction flow meters (orifice, Venturi) infer flow from pressure drop. For incompressible flow Q = Cd A2√[2Δp/(ρ(1−β⁴))], β = d2/d1. Venturi typically has lower permanent pressure loss. A magnetic flow meter uses Faraday induction: voltage proportional to magnetic flux density, electrode separation and mean fluid velocity; it needs an electrically conductive liquid and no flow obstruction.

### Worked examples

Strain gauge R = 120 Ω, GF = 2, ε = 500 microstrain = 0.0005. ΔR = 120×2×0.0005 = 0.12 Ω. A 5 V quarter bridge gives 1.25 mV before amplification. For a Pt100 with α = 0.00385/K at 80°C, R ≈ 130.8 Ω. For an ideal Venturi with A2 = 0.001 m², β = 0.5, Δp = 5,000 Pa and water ρ = 1,000 kg/m³, Q = 0.003266 m³/s before discharge coefficient correction.

### Exam practice

Draw LVDT and describe null, positive and negative displacement. Compare thermocouple, RTD, thermistor and pyrometer. Show DAQ blocks; explain amplifier and ADC roles. For a 400 Hz bandwidth, choose sampling above 800 samples/s plus anti-alias filtering.

## Module 5 — Experimental design and statistical analysis

### Why plan experiments?

Changing many machining variables at random makes it hard to tell which factor causes a result. Design of experiments (DOE) deliberately chooses settings. A factor is an input (speed, feed); a level is a setting; the response is an output (roughness). Randomization reduces systematic order effects, replication estimates noise, and blocking groups similar conditions. A full two-factor two-level experiment has four combinations (−−, +−, −+, ++). Interaction occurs when one factor's effect depends on another. Taguchi orthogonal arrays reduce the number of trials while balancing factor-level combinations; choose arrays considering degrees of freedom and possible interactions. Taguchi signal-to-noise criteria depend on whether smaller, larger or nominal response is desired.

### ANOVA and regression

ANOVA separates variation into factors and residual error. For one-way ANOVA, SStotal = Σ(y−grand mean)², SSbetween = Σni(group mean−grand mean)², SSerror = total − between. Degrees of freedom are k−1 for between, N−k for error. Mean square = SS/df; F = MSbetween/MSerror. Compare with the chosen critical F or p-value. Assumptions include independent observations, approximately normal residuals and comparable group variances. Regression fits a response equation: y = b0 + b1x + error. Least squares slope = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ)/Σ(x−x̄)²; intercept = ȳ−b1x̄. For coded factorial data add interaction term b12x1x2. Check residual plots, do not infer causation from association alone.

A probability density describes distribution of continuous measurement error; its integral over a range gives probability. Independent normal errors combine by variance addition for linear systems. Reduce bias by calibration, drift by temperature compensation, noise by shielding/filtering and repeat measurements; averaging reduces independent random uncertainty by 1/√n, not fixed bias.

### Worked example — ANOVA

Two settings give responses A = 4,5,6 and B = 8,9,10. Group means 5 and 9; grand mean 7. SSbetween = 3(5−7)²+3(9−7)² = 24. Within each group SS = 2, so SSerror = 4. df between = 1; df error = 4. MSbetween = 24, MSerror = 1, F = 24. At 5% significance F(1,4) critical is about 7.71; reject equal means under assumptions. For regression data (1,3),(2,5),(3,7), slope 2, intercept 1, predicted y at x=4 is 9 (extrapolation may be unreliable).

### Assignment and exam practice

Take actual data from a laboratory or cited research article, record settings and replicates, plot group means/error bars, perform ANOVA and interpret assumptions and results. Do not invent observed data. Explain factorial design and orthogonal arrays; calculate F from SS and df; describe techniques for reducing measurement uncertainty.
